speechtext: Yes ; I do not know whether this is the proper time to bring up the whole question or not.

It seems to me, from all I can gather, that the country generally is ripe to stop this for the time being, at least. AVe had a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway standing up in this House and telling us that he thought the time had come when railways would build their roads into the sections of the country that they thought would pay them, without any bonuses from the government. I know that in the section of the country whence I come this has been a burning question for years. They have opposed this railway bonus system for a number of years, and especially since the Patron movement started. In 1896, the Patron candidate who opposed me had as one of the principal planks in his platform, opposition to railway bonuses.

Some hon. AIEA1BERS. Hear, hear.

Aly hon. friends opposite say ' hear, hear,' but it all depends upon what you consider a good government. If a good government is a government that will break all its pledges and fail to carry out. its promises to the people, then this is a good government and no doubt the best Canada has ever seen, but if a government which does all that is a bad government then this is the worst government we have ever had.

I think the government want to know the feeling of the people in the different constituencies in reference to their railway bonus policy, and as this is early in the parliament they will have an opportunity to change their ways if they find their conduct does not meet with the approval of the people.

I will not say what I was going to about my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan). Here is what Mr. Leonard, my opponent in the last election, said :
I am not in favour of the present system of bonusing, and believe that public money should be expended only for the public good, and I shall oppose any measure calculated to enrich a private individual or corporation at the expense of the public.
He was obliged to take that position because some of the strongest men in his own party refused to support him unless he did. Then, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) wrote a letter in 1894 to a gentleman who lived in my constituency who was a prominent Patron, and Sir Richard Cartwright pointed out how absurd it was for Patrons to oppose Liberals, and he tried to show that the Patron policy and the Liberal policy were exactly the same. Sir Richard Cartwright enumerated a lot of things in which the two agreed, and amongst these was that they were against bonuses to railways. In 1894 the hon. gentleman said that the Liberal party were opposed to bonusing railways, but I have never yet heard him give an explanation, or try to give an explanation, for his changed opinions in this l'egard since then. It seems a little strange that these gentlemen on the Treasury benches changed somewhat the mode of giving bonuses when they came to power. In 1S97 they made a condition that where a railway got a bonus of over $3,200 per mile, that railway was to carry the mails for ten years free of charge. But when they came to give bonuses the next year, they changed the order a little, and they made a condition that railways should pay 3 per cent interest on the moneys advanced to them, if the government employed them1 sufficiently to earn that amount. When that Bill was going through I took occasion to ask the minister, if, in case the money was not earned in the year, would it be carried forward and charged against the company. The minister replied : That it would not. but that it would be written off. I said that was hardly a business way of doing things, and he replied : We are not doing this on business principles. Well, all through the government are not doing things on business principles. Since this government has come into office it has voted over $18,000,000 in the way of sub-Mr. BENNETT.
sidies or bonuses to railways. It is true that they have not all earned their subsidies and the subsidies have not been paid, but the government has paid out $5,883,000 on these bonuses, and they have pledged the country to pay the balance. To-day we have the government asking for a renewal of some of these subsidies that have not been earned.
In my opinion, unless the companies have earned their money the bonuses should not be renewed except for some very strong reason. I asked for a return in reference to the matter, and I find that none of the 3 per cent interest has been earned, and none of it paid. Is it possible that the government has paid out nearly $6,000,000 to railways with which they had no business to transact ? If the government had no business with these railways, how much business would the general public have with them ?
It does seem to me that these railways could have given some of the money back, if the government had mails to carry, but my impression was then, and it is now, that the government wanted to give this subsidy to the railway, and that they inserted this clause in order to make the people believe that it was only a loan although the government had no intention of living up to the spirit of the law. 1 am not going to trouble the House with reading extracts ; I will merely ask my hon. friends opposite to look at some of the Globe editorials for the year 1S97, in which it is stated plainly and above board, that these bonuses are worse than waste, that the time has come when they should be stopped, that a railway that will not pay should not be built, and that the railway business should be put on the same basis as any other business. Why is it that we have so many people coming to this parliament asking for charters ? Are they men who will build the roads or are they men who only want to get the charters for what is in them, thinking that if they get a charter they will get a bonus, and then be able to peddle the charter around and make money out of it. I want to say, as the representative of Lennox and on behalf of the people of that riding, that I am entirely opposed to this system of bonusing railways.

With regard to the observation's of my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), as they dealt with the general question of railway subsidies, I would like a word or two in reply. No doubt some years ago there were strong opinions held by many people in this country on the general question of granting railway subsidies to roads which might in a sense be called local roads. I quite understand that at the beginning of that policy there was much room for debate ; but after it has been pursued for many years, and many sections of the country have enjoyed the benefits of it, it would be most illogical, unreasonable, unjust and ungenerous to attempt 'now to restrict it, and to say that those sections of the country which have not enjoyed its benefits at all shall be debarred from those benefits, although they have contributed towards giving them to other sections. Take the ease of my hon. friend's own neighbourhood. He comes from a section of country which has been favoured with the blessings of railway communications for nearly half a century-at any rate, for thirty years or more, since the time the Grand Trunk was constructed ; and I believe, although I have not a personal knowledge of the matter, that his district is well supplied with other railways-in fact, it has practically a network of railways ; and now my hon. friend, although he and his neighbours have enjoyed the benefits of railway construction for many years, is prepared to deny those blessings to other sections. I am sure I have only to call his attention to the unfairness of his position, to enable him to see that he should not adhere to that view. Take the particular item under notice, which only serves as an illustration-the first item, for a railway which it is proposed to run through the county of Guysboro' in Nova Scotia. That is a large county, with not a

very large population, though considerable, but with large fishing, mining and agricultural interests. It is a fair type of many counties in the lower provinces. There is a railway touching the edge of that county on the way to Cape Breton, but five-sixths of the county is without the benefit of railway communication. Prom the time of Confederation down to the present time the people of that county have contributed their mite to pay for the railroads which my hon. friend has enjoyed in the town of Napanee ; and would it be fair or reasonable for my hon. friend, after having enjoyed those blessings, and made the whole Dominion pay for them, now to turn round and deny to my hon. friend from Guysboro' the same blessings, when he has the opportunity, after many years of waiting, to get a railroad through his county ? My hon. friend says he will see whether they paid for their railroads. I would remind him that the contributions of the old provinces of Canada to the Grand Trunk form a portion of the debt of Canada, which is placed on the shoulders of the whole Dominion, and to which we are all contributing our share. I venture to say that whatever differences of opinion there may have been in former years, in regard to this policy, there are none now ; and though it was quite fair and logical for a man to take exception to the policy of granting these railway subsidies in the beginning, yet now, when that policy has been pursued for many years, and many sections of the Dominion have enjoyed tire benefits of it, you cannot go back on it, but are bound to recognize it as the fixed policy of Canada ; so that, wherever there is an undeveloped section of Canada-be it in the east, west, north or south-if they are likely to get a railway by the aid of the moderate subsidy which this government grants, I do not see how any government can do otherwise than grant it. In that respect we do not differ from hon. gentlemen opposite.
Hear, hear.

It may be that here and there some individual member of the House feels free to express his individual views, but let us understand clearly that this policy of railway subsidies, now and in recent years, has been the fixed policy of both parties, and that the very resolutions the hon. gentleman complains of as granting large subsidies, have, during the last three or four years, been supported by both sides, and I challenge my hon. friend tq point to any vote he ever gave against them. They were passed by the general consent of the House, either unanimously or without division. They are the fixed policy of the country, and so long as that policy is applied with moderation and a desire to serve the sections still requiring railway development, that is a policy which any government may be proud to present to the people of Canada.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman could not have felt very comfortable in his reply to my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), when seated beside him as one of his colleagues who, in 1896, wrote to the Farmer's Son, the then organ of the Patrons, that the policy of the Reform party was practically that laid down by the Patrons of Industry, one of the planks in whose platform was no more subsidies to railways. The Finance Minister, by his plea, has just condemned his colleague for the principles laid down in that letter. Surely the hon. member for Lennox was, under the circumstances, justified in drawing attention to the fact that hon. gentlemen on the Treasury benches have gone back on their platform.
The hon. minister referred to the debt of the Grand Trunk Railway, of which every province has to pay its share, and he asked were not the maritime provinces, therefore, entitled to some consideration in the way of bonuses. But, Sir, he omitted to mention the fact that the Intercolonial Railway is a road built specially to accommodate the maritime provinces, and that all the other provinces pay their share of the debt. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, and the Intercolonial Railway are all Dominion works, and consequently each province has its share of their benefits as well as their debts. But what we complain of is that the policy of the government is in open violation of its platform in 1893. I am not opposing in the main the policy of assisting railways. What I claim to be the correct principle is to subsidize such lines as open up new sections of country not yet supplied by railways. There are portions of the country which have never had the benefit of railway facilities, and which do not offer sufficient inducements to capitalists to build. It is the duty of the government to come to the assistance of the people, who are entitled to these conveniences of civilization just as are the people in other sections of the country. But the general necessity for the granting of subsidies does not exist to the same extent to-day as it did some years ago. Money is to-day more plentiful, and our mining enterprises and pulp and other industries offer stronger inducements to capitalists to invest their money in the building of railways. Therefore, we ought to be much more careful in the granting of subsidies than we were twenty-five years ago. I think the time has come when it would be wise for us to grant assistance to railway enterprises on the plan adopted by our American neighbours, namely, by giving them loans which would be repayable some time in the future. But we certainly, in any case, should avoid giving indiscriminate subsidies all over the country, and confine them to the newer sections of country which, without such assistance, would remain undeveloped.

Another tiling to which I would draw attention is the amount of the subsidy. We propose to give $3,200 per mile as the lowest subsidy to railways, which do not cost over $15,000 a mile. But any one will understand how easy it is for a railway company to show that its line has cost over $15,000 a mile, and if the cost exceeds $15,000 per mile, then the company is entitled to ask for an additional subsidy of $3,200 per mile, making in all $6,400. What means does the government take to check the accounts furnished by the railway companies. The same remark applies to bridges. We propose to give a subsidy of 15 per cent on the cost of a bridge provided that bridge costs over a certain sum. But how does that system work? We h(id an application for that subsidy from the company which built the Sorel bridge on the South Shore. They gave a statement of the cost, $243,000. It appears, however, that some parties were satisfied that the bridge did not cost that amount, and we find in the Auditor General's Report various estimates. Mr. C. A. Keefer estimated the cost at $112,472. Mr. Sclireiber took Mr. Keefer's quantities and gave a different estimate altogether. Mr. McCarthy, the engineer of the company, made the cost $150,,084, and Mr. Ridout estimated it at $101,000. Yet upon the strength of the claim which was entered by the company, the government is expected to pay a subsidy of 15 per cent. What check have the government that would justify us in the belief that they' are not paying on more than the actual cost? We have no check that could be regarded as final and concluding. I would advise the government to devise means of checking the accounts of these companies, or otherwise we will be paying them larger subsidies than they are entitled to.

The statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) with regard to this resolution is not correct. He stated that this gave a subsidy of $3,200 per mile to a railway costing $15,000 a mile, and that if it cost more than that it received an additional $3,200. That is not the resolution. The resolution states that a railway receiving $15,000 a mile shall receive a bonus of $3,200 a mile, but in any case no railway shall receive more than $6,400 a mile.
Mi-. SPROULE. Does not the resolution say that it shall not exceed $6,400 a mile ?

I shall read the resolution, as I intended to do in the first place :
Resolved, that it is expedient to authorize the Governor in Council to grant a subsidy of $3,200 per mile towards the construction of each of the undermentioned lines of railway (not exceeding in any case the number of miles hereinafter respectively stated), which shall not cost more on the average than $15,000 per mile for the mileage subsidized, and towards the construction of each of the said lines of railway not exceeding the mileage hereinafter stated, which shall cost more on the average than $15,000 per mile for the mileage subsidized, a further
subsidy beyond the sum of $3,200 per mile of fifty per centum on so much of the average cost of the mileage subsidized as shall be in excess of $15,000 per mile, such subsidy not exceeding in the whole the sum of $6,400 per mile.
Will tlie bon. gentleman tell me wherein I am incorrect ?

The hon. gentleman is entirely incorrect. Suppose a road cost $16,000 per mile, the subsidy it receives will be $6,400 per mile, plus one-half the cost over $15,000 per mile or $500. Now, I certainly think it unkind for some of the hon. gentlemen from certain constituencies to find fault with the granting of these subsidies. It is very well to make general statements that we must be careful how these subsidies are being granted to see that they are given only to deserving roads. I take it for granted that the government have been careful to see to that. I know of no railway on this list that is not deserving, and I have not heard any lion, gentleman refer to. any particular item and say that such is not the case. I think it is ungenerous as well as unjust for hon. gentlemen whose constituencies have been served not merely with subventions to railways, but with large sums for the construction of canals and other important public works to come here and say : We have got all we want, and now we will close the door on further expenditure of this kind.
1 The hon. gentleman's own friends said that.

If the hon. gentleman will pardon me, he has taken the long way around to show what my friends stated. Before the Liberal party came into power, they laid down a platform on which they asked the confidence of the people. We are responsible for our platform, I for one do not care to listen to quotations from what some gentleman may have said which was reported in some newspaper and is not held to be the policy for the Liberal party to-day. Our policy is what it has been, and, I hope, what it will be in the future- that subsidies shall be given to deserving railways.
Is the hon. gentleman ashamed of the policy proclaimed by his leaders in the past ? Does he repudiate the utterances of his friends ?

I am neither ashamed of, nor do I repudiate anything that has been said by anybody for whom I am not responsible-I have nothing to do with that one way or the other. I hold with the) policy of the party as enunciated by the party and laid down by the party. I stand by the utterances of the leaders of my party in parliament. But I am not going to be held by the remarks of some newspaper published in the wilds of Ontario. I was struck by the remarks of the hon. gentleman from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock).

Toronto, I find, is a generous city. They *have had nothing done for them from the general funds of the Dominion ; they have not been built up from the money of this country spent in the construction of railways and canals. But what struck me most forcibly was the parental care with which this hon. gentleman wished to take from the government all power and responsibility in these matters. He wanted a railway commission to take the matter out of the hands of the government and consider these questions, carefully, critically, dispassionately, and decide when a railway subsidy should be granted. X can understand why the hon. gentleman is anxious to get as much power out of the hands of the government as he can ; but he did not seem to be worried on that score when his own party was in power. So far as I am concerned, I am prepared to believe that the government as it exists is in quite as good a position to decide when a railway should have a subsidy as any commission that might he formed for that purpose. Now, we hear of huckstering charters. In our province of Nova Scotia and in the maritime provinces generally, we have seen very little of that. I have heard a great deal of talk about it up here, but have seen very few instances of it. I do not think it is well' for us in this way or in any way to discourage the building of railways. I agree with what has frequently been said this session that the great question before us to-day, the question which involves the greatness of Canada more than any other, perhaps more than all others, is the question of transportation. This question we should not regard from a sectional standpoint, but we should work together to settle in the best interests of the country this greatest of all questions that we have to deal with.

Since my entrance into parliament I have consistently opposed the bonusing of railways. I believe that the system is entirely vicious, and I hold, with the Globe, that the time has come when we should inaugurate a new system with regard to railways.
The present Globe ?

Yes, the present Globe. The people of Canada have contributed for the construction of railroads ?223,000,000, exclusive of anything we may vote this session. We have given 60,000,000 acres of land, and if you include the exemption from taxation of these lands, hon. gentlemen will understand what an enormous subsidy that means. If you take the lands at $3 an acre, you get $180,000,000 worth of land grants, or, in all, some $403,000,000. This is the sum that the people of Canada have contributed for the construction of railways-practically enough to Mr. WADE.
build all the railroads in Canada at the present time.
Instead of controlling these railroads, these railroads exercise a very important control over parliament. We have not got that control of rates that we should have. The whole transportation question, to my mind, has been bungled from the start. These remarks will apply equally to our canal system. I think, with the hon. member from Toronto (Mr. Brock) and with the others who have studied this question, that the time has come for the inauguration of a new policy with regard to railroads. I am not here to say that no railroad should be built, but I say that if the country is to go on as it has been going for the .last twenty years, paying for these railroads without owning them, and if we are to give large bonuses as we have been doing, these bonuses ought to be given under an entirely different system. We ought to make conditions, so that if at any time we desired to take these roads over, we can take them over, less the bonuses we have given. Then, we ought to exercise most careful supervision over the bonding of these railroads, over the capitalization that may be made upon them ; so that when the time comes, as come it will, when the railroads of this country must be nationalized, we will be able to nationalize them on a proper basis.
I listened with great regret to the remarks of the hon. the Minister of Finance when he declared that we have in this country the same policy carried out by both parties, Now, as a Liberal from childhood up, I wan t to dissent from that view. That is not wha t I learned from the Liberal party. I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued in 1896 by the Liberal party, entitled: 'Dominion of Canada -Principles, Policy and Platform of the Liberal Party.' I turn to page 53, and I find, in a discussion of the Patron platform, a paragraph which I will read. This is the campaign document which was placed before the people. I will read clause 11 of the Patron platform, and what the writer of the platform says of it:
Clause 11. Prohibition of the bonusing of railways by government grants, as contrary to the public interest.
The policy of bonusing railways by cash and land grants from the Dominion government has become a fruitful source of jobbery, speculation and corruption. Under its operation favourites of the government have been enriched. Appropriations have been made for the sole purpose of purchasing the support of constituencies, and vast sums of public money have been voted without regard to the public interest, while millions of acres of land that should have been held in trust by the government for the future homes of hardy and deserving settlers, have beeu handed over without consideration or justification, to charter hawkers, whose intervention actually retards the construction of the lines whose franchises they control, for the purpose of extorting money from the ultimate builders of the roads. The policy of granting these subsidies has repeatedly been condemned

in parliament by the Liberal party, and this resolution is in harmony with the attitude of the Liberal party upon this question. (See resolutions 3 and 6, Liberal platform.)
Who signs that?

This was issued by the Liberal organizer of Ontario in 1896, for distribution over the entire country. On the first page I read :
Copies of this pamphlet can be had by Liberal candidates from Alexander Smith, Secretary, Ontario Liberal Association, 34 Victoria street, Toronto.
Now, I do not read this for the purpose of giving any party in this House any comfort, for the policy which has been followed by the Conservative party in regard to bonus-ing railways has been an iniquitous policy, in my estimation, and I cannot denounce it too strongly. The claim I make is that the Liberal party was returned to power after having denounced that policy ; and I regretted to hear the Minister of Finance make the statement, that the policy of the two parties was now the same in this respect. I certainly did not learn that policy at the feet of the Liberal party. I want to say, also, that every word expressed in that resolution which I have just read I agren with. I agreed with it in 1890. and I agree with it to-day. I think that the history of railway subsidies since 1896 has been as vicious as it was prior to that date. The position I took then I take to-day ; and 1 would urge upon the government the desirability of inaugurating a new policy with regard to the bonusing of railroads and the control of railroads. 1 believe you will never have the transportation question in this country satisfactorily solved until the government controls at least one railroad extending from the Atlantic and reaching into the wheat fields of the North-west Territories.
Now. whatever may be said in favour of bonusing or assisting railroad construction, say, in the province of British Columbia, or even in the settled portions of the Northwest Territories, I think it is utterly indefensible that in this year of grace, 1901, this parliament should be called upon to vote vast subsidies for the purpose of building railroads in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and many portions of the province of Quebec. Why, these provinces have been settled two or three hundred years, and surely they ought to be able to stand upon their own feet in the matter of transportation, and this House ought not to be called upon to furnish subsidies to help build these railroads. Fancy a proposition being made in the United States Congress for subsidizing railroads ; why, it would be laughed out of court. Surely, we ought to learn some lessons in this country, and one thing we ought to learn is, that it is time, if we are going to contribute practically all the money, all the resources that we have been giving towards these railroads, that the parliament of Canada should exercise efficient control over them. I do not profess to be a prophet, but I say that within five years, so strongly will the opinion of the people of Canada be aroused upon this question,- that the government, be it Liberal or Conservative, will be forced to take up this question in a practical manner and to see that the money that the people are contributing for the building of these railroads is not wasted, and that if we build them, we should at least have them operated in the interest of the people who contribute the money.

I would not speak on this occasion were it not for the reference to the railway in my own county. I will ease the hon. gentleman's suspicion that there is any corruption in this, when I state that since 1867 the county of Guysborough has on only one occasion returned a Conservative to the House of Commons. So it cannot be for the purpose of purchasing votes in my county, for my county has always returned Liberals except on that one occasion. Neither can it be for the purpose of rewarding political supporters, because the company that are now going to build this railroad is composed of M. H. Fitzpatrick, the local Conservative member of the House of Assembly in Nova Scotia, one of the best men I know, and Mr. George McCormick, who sits in this House and is a gentleman who cannot be purchased by giving him a grant to a railway. This, at least, can stand on its merits. It was voted before, and voted without objection. The county is a very large one, is rich in natural resources, and I think that while we may be at some pains to examine these votes closely, as the hon. member for East Grey says, when a good case is made out, the proper position to take is, that the subsidy should be granted. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson, Lisgar) who has just spoken has forgotten the fact of the immense sums the United States had to pay for the construction of railways. Take, for instance, the Union and Central Pacific.
Yes, but they got it all back.
They have not got it back to this day. How about the land grants ?
They got the money back. They made the Union Pacific pay the money back.
They ran the road into bankruptcy.
One hundred millions has been paid back to the American government.
The granting of a subsidy to that road was necessary at the time.
We must impose conditions here also.

The hon, gentleman (Mr. Richardson, Lisgar) forgets that in the United States matters are reversed from the position in which they are in this country. In the United States a great transcontinental railway will receive assistance, hut the United States government has nothing to do with railways in the several states. Each state is in an independent position, while our province has only a small subsidy out of which it cannot grant railway subsidies.

Will the hon.
gentleman say that any state in the union grants cash subsidies ?

I am not saying so, but I am giving that reason to show why the central government has not voted large amounts of money. In the United States the country is so rich that the question there is as to who shall he allowed to build) the railways. Does the hon. gentleman say that the Canadian Pacific Railway would ever have been built without being paid something to assist it in opening up the richest country in the world, a part of country where ten acres of land is worth a farm of one liunderd acres in the lower provinces, and if you give a grant to the richest part of the country that you have in Manitoba are you going to deny it to a smaller province ?
Where is all this going to lead to if we accept the dictum of the hon. Minister of Finance that because one section of the country has got it others have a right to claim it ?

If a good case is made out. certainly, but the Dominion) has a mighty margin yet before it will get to the time when it has given to other roads the amount which has been voted to the Canadian Pacific Railway to build a road in the hon. gentleman's country.
I think it would have been better if it had been built in accordance with the policy laid down by Mr. Mackenzie.

We will not discuss that now. The hon. gentleman and I may agree upon that, but that is not the question we are discussing now. We have to do with conditions as they exist now. and not go back to what would have been wise at another time more than to draw from joast experience a lesson as to what it is wise for us to do at the present. I have my own views, I am not sure but that in a well populated country the future may not call for the government ownership of railways. I regret that just now I do not see very much hope for the adoption of that principle in Canada-not for a number of years at least. The whole subsidy given to these roads is only one-fifth of what they could be built for. The subsidy is $3,200 a mile, and I venture to say that not less than $15,000 a Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
mile will build any of these roads. The hon. gentleman showed conclusively that $400,000 had been given by this country.
Including land grants.

I will accept the hon. gentleman's statement. If you are to get back the roads which have been built and for which subsidies have been granted, this country will have to provide at once cash to the amount of $2,000,000,000. Is not that a large sum ? Four hundred millions multiplied by five would make two thousand millions. Is this country ready to borrow $2,000,000,000 to take over the railways ?
All you have to do is to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) and buy the stock. He said you could control the Canadian Pacific for $5,000.

He said you could control the stock for $2. I will not adopt that suggestion, because it is not correct. There is no man who will seriously look at the question of transportation to-day but must be struck with this fact, that if a country is thickly populated, the right thing may be for the country to own the railways ; but with an extent of country, such as we have from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and with the sparse population we have, I do not see how the country can undertake that just now. I have a very high respect for the judgment of my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), but I cannot help saying that with the otium cum dignitate of the county of Lennox, with plenty of railways, with the St. Lawrence beside it, and with the $11,000,000 that the present government have spent to make the St. Lawrence better, it should be kind to poorer and less favoured people. It ought to be happy that other parts of the country should be as highly favoured as it has been. I have, in my county with 200 miles of seashore, only two miles of railway. I am pleased to think that these men are ready to put their capital with the subsidy to build that road. There are natural advantages in the county. There is wood, mineral, fish and there is quite a large part of it fairly good farming land. Well, now. is it not a good thing to do to encourage those who are opening up the country ? Do not suppose that I am for giving indiscriminately because there is the asking; but if a fair case is made out, I submit that for years to come we will have to consider it. I think the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) misunderstood me when he spoke about a railway commission. My idea of a commission is not at all to say whether a road is to be built 10 or 20 miles long, but to a commission to be appointed to solve the great and difficult question of transportation from one end of the country to the other. It is not that a commission should be appointed to be sent down to my part of the country, for instance, to say

whether 10 or 20 miles of road should be built.
I did uot say that they should decide as to whether 10 miles of railway should be built or not, but I said that they should determine whether the road is in the public interest.

A gentleman from Toronto, for example, looks out and sees a great city, and he goes out ten miles and he sees a well-populated rich district. Then, he comes down to Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, where there are ten miles of road to be built, and he says : It is shameful to have a road built here, while from the ground, out of the forests, and the fisheries wealth may be taken that he never dreamed of.
Let them pay for it and not the whole country.

That is to say that the man who has to dig for a wage in the mine should not be assisted at all. My idea of parliament is to give assistance to the weaker. This country, if it is ever going to become great, must assist the poorer people and not lavish bounties upon a few individuals
The hon. gentleman was speaking of great wealth in mines, timber and land. If the wealth is there let them pay for the railway.

I was speaking of the great wealth. I said there might be wealth there. Suppose there is a good iron mine 20 miles from railway communication ; you are not going to get capitalists to go in there and build a railway when elsewhere they have a road to as good an iron mine already built, and all they have to do is to pay the freight on their product. Has the man who has to dig in the mine to pay out of his own pocket for a railway, while at another place a railway is already built ? The hon. gentleman, I have no doubt, would stand up and say that a factory which had declared a dividend of 15 per cent should get further protection, but he will not say that the people who live without any advantages should be assisted by subventions. We are now having a recoil from the system that has prevailed in this country in the past. It was a system of assisting particular individuals. I am in favour of a system of bounties which will assist the larger number. For five or six years I have been trying to get this subvention for a railway in my county, but I have not been so successful as I had hoped I would be. Now, I say that we will be more successful, and if a good case is made out to assist those who need assistance, I care not in what part of the Dominion that place may be, I will vote for it.
What is the total of the applications for subsidies filed with the government this year, and what proportion has been conceded ? The minister can give it in the rough.
I have not added up the whole amount, but I think somewhere in the neighbourhood of $18,000,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And you are giving how much ?

Between $3,000,000 and $4,000,000. I do not think that very much is to be gained on either side of the House by quoting the utterances of individual members of parliament, no matter how prominent they may be. I apprehend that on a question of this kind you will always discover a very great difference of opinion amongst members within the ranks of both political organizations. I take it that the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) has by no means expressed the views of a large proportion, not to speak of the majority, of the political friends with which he is associated. It therefore would not be fairly stating the attitude of gentlemen opposite to quote the member for Lennox as having expressed their views. I conceive that there is quite a little feeling in the country of uncertainty as to the wisdom of our continuing to grant' year after year subsidies to railways as has been done in the past.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was not that feeling catered to by the Liberal party ?

My hon. friend may be correct or ihe may not. The chances are that, without the action of any political party, the people themselves would be inclined to think that it is well to be exceedingly cautious and prudent in respect to the granting of railway subsidies. The government in their submission to parliament on the present occasion have been influenced by the feeling that we should exercise the utmost care and satisfy ourselves that the particular railways we are aiding are meritorious undertakings, and are going to be of permanent advantage to the country. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) has made us a suggestion. He, coming from Toronto, does not appreciate the needs of sections of the country which have been without railway communication, and I venture to think- though I may be doing the hon. gentleman an injustice-that he has not considered the suggestion which he himself has made. He thinks that the origin of the difficulty is in the readiness with which charters are granted for railways, and he has gone so far as to conclude that we should put some restriction upon the granting of charters. He believes that a commission ought to be constituted by parliament ; a commission that would be composed of most exemplary, independent and capable men, and that they should be called upon to advise parliament

as to whether or not this, that or the other railway application should be entertained. If my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) had carried his consideration further, I think he would have seen that parliament would be very unlikely to have its judgment influenced upon a question of that importance by the opinions of any four or five of the most capable men that the country could produce. My hon. friend (Mr, Brock) shakes his head, but nevertheless I think he is wrong in the opinion he has expressed. I do not believe that parliament would be prepared to abrogate its functions and to refuse to exercise its own judgment upon a question of that kind. If parliament were to constitute a commission whose duty it would be to advise parliament as to whether or not a railway should be chartered in this direction or that, parliament would be more likely to be influenced by the members who would represent that or the adjacent districts than it would be by the conclusion of any such commission. My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) thinks he might not be influenced himself, but I believe he would be just as ready to be influenced by the opinions of members of parliament in whom he had confidence as by the opinion of any outside commission. I think I know my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman is exceedingly alarmed about the present condition of affairs. He says that the country is granting these subsidies as they had been granted for years past. My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) has denounced the expenditures which have been made in times past. He denounces the expenditure on the Trent canal, which he says is pure waste of money, and he intimates that is his view with regard to many railway subsidies which have been granted. My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) is in the position that he does not unshackle his mind until he gets into opposition. For^ years my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) was, as he is to-day, one of the most ardent, one of the most determined, one of the most-shall I say unreasoning, when it comes to his political opponents-one of the strongest adherents of the Conservative party. All his life he has loyally and faithfully. and no doubt conscientiously, supported all the measures of the Conservative government. He supported them in what he calls this outrageous expenditure on the Trent canal. It did not shake the hon. gentleman a hair. He was just as ceaseless a supporter of the Conservative party then as he is now when they are in opposition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Who says it was an outrageous expenditure ?
I am quoting the hon. gentleman from Toronto.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And he has not apologized.

He ought. My hon. friend (Mr. Mr. BLAIR.
Brock), as the candidate of the party who committed these atrocities, went on the public platform and defended them to the utmost extent, or he would not be here. My hon. friend must realize tnat as a member of parliament he is in a different position from that which he has occupied all his life before. He needs a larger view of questions than he took before. And what he in his conscience thought all right, in that altered conscience-I am not going to say it is an improved conscience-he finds everything here wrong. If my hon. friend were to move that the question as to whether a charter should be granted and a railway subsidy given should be referred to a very intelligent commission, even of his own choice, I do not think that many of his political friends would support him. And why ? Because members of parliament who have had experience in these things know that you cannot pursue a particular line of policy which has benefited one section of the country without following it up for a reasonable time, so that all sections of the country may participate in the advantages. My hon. friend has not had practical experience enough
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You mean log rolling.

My hon. friend calls it log rolling. He calls it log rolling when it is done by this side of the House, but he would call it the highest standard of propriety of conduct if it were done by his political friends. It is a machine when we do it; it is a fine high-toned organization when they do it. I do not want to say anything offensive to my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) because I know he is a very respectable gentleman, and one who has secured the respect of the community in which he lives. Therefore I do not like to say what I might say even in parliamentary terms regarding him.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Thank you.

Coming to the question of the subsidies, the hon. gentleman from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) thinks we should adopt the course pursued in the United States. He does not say that we should stop granting subsidies at once. Reasonable gentleman, my hon. friend from Grey. He thinks we ought to confine the policy to meritorious undertakings. We are entirely with his opinion about that. Let us see whether we can agree further. The hon. gentleman says that we ought to give loans as they do in the United States. I do not know whether there is any uniform 'system of aiding railways in force in the United States. I know that in many states they do not give aid as a system. I know that the municipal bodies do, when they are interested in railways. I believe that the government of the United States has done so in the past in very notable instances, but I do not think it is doing so at present. But if you adopt the plan of

making loans to companies, you would require to tliink it out pretty well.
Suppose we say we would make a loan to assist the construction of a railway in a desirable section of the country, we would have to consider on what principle we would make that loan. Are we going to make that loan in such a way as to ensure the construction of this particular work? If we are, we have practically to loan them all the money the undertaking will cost. Or are you only going to loan them a part? If you are, and they have to borrow the balance elsewhere, you will have to take a second lien on the railway ; for if the government attempted to take a first mortgage for its loan, that would certainly prevent the company procuring a second loan on a second mortgage, because nobody would advance money under such circumstances. Ton would either have to arrange that, your loan would be for the whole amount, or if it were only for a portion, you would have to subordinate the government loan to the loan the company would make in the money market. Now, if you are going to take a second mortgage, under what conditions will you take it? How will you regulate the amount for which the first mortgage will be given? The first mortgage might be given for a very much larger sum than the company would need to borrow. If it were to toe limited to the amount required with the government subsidy to construct the road, you would have to limit it in some such way as to prevent the company making an excessive loan in priority to the government loan. You would have to have some machinery for that purpose, and that. I apprehend, Would not be an easy task. It is not an easy matter to devise a working scheme by which the loan business could be managed by the government. I have thought of the matter a good deal, and I would be prepared to secure on tiie undertaking every dollar the government might advance by way of subsidy ; but you must not kill the undertaking in endeavouring to get security for the government, because the object is to encourage and promote the construction of the particular work in question. You must devise your plan in such a way that, while it will secure the government, it will at the same time ensure the object you have in view in making the grant, namely, the successful carrying out of the undertaking. That, as I have said, is not a thing that can be very easily arranged. It is a thing which demands a good deal of consideration, and it might lead to a great deal of trouble in working it out. So that when my bon. friend suggests the idea of a loan, I want him to understand that the matter has not toy any means escaped the very serious consideration of the government, and it will continue to receive our consideration in the hope that we may be able to devise some plan for securing the return of the whole or the portion of these aids, to the public exchequer.
Now, my hon. friend has pointed out that it is by no means an easy matter to work out that portion of the policy of the government which provides that when the cost of the work does not exceed $15,000 a mile, the subsidy shall be limited to $3,200 a mile, and that the company constructing the line contracted for with the government shall be entitled to 50 per cent of the excess over $15,000 ; and he has said that in the working out of this plan it has been found a very easy thing for companies to secure the additional subsidy, notwithstanding the provisions we have made. I think my hon. friend has lost sight of the object and purpose we have in view in devising this method of adjusting the subsidies. The hon. member knows that in times past a great many subsidies were given in aid of railways for very much larger amounts than $3,200 per mile. Some subsidies were given up to the full extent of $12,000, some at $10,000, I think some at $8,000. At all events, they ran all the way from $3,200 up to $12,000 a mile.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Where do you find that information? I only know of two roads that received a subsidy of over $3,200 a mile : that is the Canada Central, and the road to connect Toronto with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
My hon. friend has forgotten the subsidies which have been given. There are a number of roads which received much larger subsidies than $3,200.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There were some subsidies telescoped, and there were certain roads in the North-west which were granted so much per year.
What does telescoping mean?
It is a plan by which the subsidy is doubled up on a particular section of a road.

I can give the hon. gentleman a list of the subsidies, and when he sees it, he will be surprised if he thinks at this moment that there were only two or three roads which were given more than $3,200 a mile. There was no apparent principle on which the aid was granted ; but we did feel that, in order that the railway companies that were receiving aid from us should know that they were toeing dealt with upon an equal and fair principle, we could accomplish that by some such sliding scale, according to cost, as we have provided here; and it has not been so easy a matter as the hon. member supposes for railway companies to obtain the additional subsidy. I brought down a statement last session showing the total number of railway companies which had received aid in excess of $3,200 per mile, under the operation of this sliding scale, and, if my memory serves me,

there were only three that secured the additional aid. I cannot recollect that any company since last session has been receiving more than .$3,200 per mile. There were only three, at the outside, when the statement was brought down last year, that received more.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There was the Rainy River road.
That did not receive its subsidy under the sliding scale. I am speaking of those which were included in the sliding scale.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In the return brought down last year there is nothing to show that any of the companies received more than $3,200 per mile, although some did.
There was nothing in the resolution calling for such information.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that he brought down a return last year showing this.

I do not know whether I brought a return or not; but I made the statement in parliament when the subsidies were under consideration. I had the information and gave it to parliament, and the hon. gentleman will find it In ' Hansard.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman prepared to lay on the Table a map of each province where subsidies are now being granted, showing the probable cost of each line? The hon. gentleman does not expect the committee to assent to his resolution until he puts them in possession of that reasonable measure of information?

If my hon. friend waits until wo have maps of all the provinces, I am afraid his anticipation will not be realized of spending at home his holiday on the 24th of May. I do not think that the hon. gentleman has ever heard of any such detailed and voluminous information having been supplied in other years. I do not think my predecessor will say it is customary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Always, every time.
I think that my hon. friend's memory is in fault. I could not promise to furnish the information asked for at this late period.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not think it is open for the hon. gentleman to excuse himself because of the late period at which he brings down these resolutions. He brings them very late, and then makes that unfortunate circumstance the ground for refusing any information to the committee. Let me point the hon. gentleman to the doctrine which one of his colleagues laid down Mr. BLAIR.
with regard to this matter. In 1S90, his hon. colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, said:
I say that no government which was true to the country would grant one of these railways a subsidy until there were first laid before the Minister of Railways and submitted to parliament, sufficiently fair and accurate plans of the country to be traversed to enable the minister and the House to form a reasonably accurate estimate of the total cost of the road.
No government true to the country would do otherwise. That was the opinion in 1890 of the gentleman who now occupies the position of Minister of Trade and Commerce. I suppose he has not changed his views, and therefore will not regard this government as true to the interests of the country. He laid down the further principle :
In the second place, evidence should be given to the minister, and should be transmitted by him to parliament, to show that the parties in connection with it had reasonable facilities and reasonable means to enable them to construct the line ; that they were not men of straw. The hon. gentleman comes down with this resolution, and has not said a word with regard to the prospect of carrying out any one of these projects. And then, Sir, the third proposition that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce laid down is particularly applicable to this case, and it was supported in even stronger language by the right hon. gentleman who now leads this House. It is as follows
Lastly, Sir, and, perhaps as important as any, it is a gross violation of all propriety and of all constitutional rule and precedence that these propositions to grant subsidies to railways should not be laid on the Table of this House several weeks before prorogation, in order that we may have time to examine them. We must go on with this policy in order that we may have time to ascertain which are reasonable and fair applications likely to benefit the country, and which, on the other hand, are likely to result in disaster and injury.
Then, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce went on with a remark which is perfectly applicable to the course which has been adopted by the Minister of Railways and Canals now :
In this present case, it is perfectly apparent that every one of these conditions were utterly disregarded.
The Minister of Railways and Canals has utterly disregarded every one of these wise suggestions of his colleague, in bringing down these resolutions. He has not furnished a plan or any evidence of the reasonableness of the enterprise, and he has brought the resolutions down a few days before prorogation. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce is not the only authority on this subject that I can quote. The right hon. gentleman who leads the government used almost violent language jn 1894 with regard to this matter. He said :
The session has lasted four months, and the government have had more time than. was ne-

cessary to prepare these resolutions. How is it possible that this House can discuss these resolutions intelligently, covering as they do about sixty different railway schemes, and involving an amount aggregating over three million dollars ? It is quite impossible under such circumstances that any man in this House can give intelligent attention to this question.
Well, the right lion, gentleman is leader of a government which, under circumstances of this kind, is bringing down between $3,000,000 and $4,000,000 of railway subsidies within a few days of prorogation. Did these lion, gentlemen believe what they were saying six years ago, or is there any reason that is applicable now that was not applicable in 1894 to a case of this kind ? The present Minister of Justice raised his voice in the same strain. He said :
We are here in the fifth month of the session *-the fifth month began this week-and we have for the first time brought under our attention a number of railway projects, the merits of which we have no opportunity to consider.
The House had as much opportunity to consider the resolutions in 1894 as the hon. gentleman affords us at the present time. Why is it, when these excellent principles were laid down so strongly by hon. gentlemen opposite, that we find the leader of the government, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce and the present Minister of Railways and Canals pursuing that course which they condemned so vigorously six years ago ? The Minister of Trade and Commerce on that same occasion said-and I invite the hon. gentleman's attention to the language he used :
More than that, every human being knows that this practice of putting these railway resolutions off until the end of the session is carried out for the express purpose of stifling and preventing inquiry.
Is the hon. gentleman of that opinion still ? And, if so, how does he justify his taking part in a policy which brings these resolutions down within a few days of prorogation ? Is it for the purpose of stifling and preventing inquiry ? The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce owes it to the House to explain why he did not, as a member of the government, insist, as he argued in 1890 and 1894, that these resolutions would be brought down a reasonable time before prorogation, should be brought down at a time when the House can properly investigate them upon evidence presented for the purpose by the government. The present Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) used even stronger language, which I could read to the House if I cared to do so. A former member of the House, Mr. McMullen, used language which went far in the same direction, but, I will not weary the House by quoting it. How comes it that we have these resolutions brought down thus late in the session, and with no evidence which would enable the House properly to judge of the value of these propositions.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) surely does not contend that because I am not able to produce maps of the different provinces showing all the railways subsidies for which have been applied for, as well as the connecting railways, that, therefore, we have not full information with regard to all these roads ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Well, give it to us.

How can the hon. gentleman reasonably ask that these plans for any particular line should be given when we are discussing another line altogether ? We have commenced at resolution No. 1, and we are still at resolution No. 1.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Well, give us the facts concerning No. 1. The hon. gentleman has not given us a particle of information.
The hon. gentleman has not given me an opportunity.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
do not think it a very creditable way for the government to adopt.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at 3 p.m.
I think the committee is entitled to some explanation on this first resolution. We .would like to know the particulars of this vote.

This is a revote. I do not think the hon. gentleman expects us to go over all the explanations that were made last year on these votes. This is identically the same railway that was subsidized the previous session, except that instead of starting from Sunnybrae, on the Intercolonial Railway, it starts from New Glasgow.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We have no map or no knowledge of the locality. The minister stated that this is a revote. That does not make any difference. In the first place, it is a different railway. He says it is, because it starts from one point on the Intercolonial Railway instead of from another point, and goes presumably to a different Diace.
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. No, It goes to exactly the same place.

Last session these votes were pushed through without explanations, but because we could not get explanations last year there is no reason why we should not get them now. The minister is bound to give the information. I think he said he would lay the papers on the Table. Has he put any papers on the Table of the House that will give us information that would justify us in passing this vote? Last year we did not get the particulars and we want them now.

The hon. gentleman is in error, he did get the information. Of course, wheu a gentleman asks for information and keeps on asking until he is told there is no further information, we can apprehend that it is not facts he wants but simply to make delay and trouble. Now, last year correspondence was brought*down in regard to this and the other votes, full explanations were given, we had the maps here, we went over them together at the Table, and all these votes were explained in a way so satisfactory that there was but one subsidy in the whole list of resolutions that was challenged on the other side. It is hardly fair for the hon. gentleman to make such a statement now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The vote is exactly the same as last year, except that last year the railway leaves at a point on the Intercolonial Railway called Sunnybrae. It was to go for a small distance over the Intercolonial Railway. The company that are now

building it means to leave from New Glasgow, some miles to the east of where It was to leave before. They think it will be a better line, but it will go to the same place. The only change in the vote now is that in place of saying, At or near Sunnybrae, it is at or near New Glasgow. New Glasgow is quite a railway centre, the short line from Oxford goes there, then the road that goes to Pictou, and another road that goes to Pictou Landing-four roads converge there. It is the centre of the steel works operations. About seven-eighths of a mile from New Glasgow there is a colliery, and the idea is to go out by that colliery and run practically over the same country for about fifteen miles. It will then strike on exactly the same line as if it left Sunnybrae.
Is it the same parties who are back of both schemes ?

Yes, and they got their charter. I may say they are about the same parties. I mentioned Mr. Fitzpatrick. Two of the shareholders are in this House, Mr. McCormick and Mr. McLeod. They are at the back of it, they are to build twenty-five miles this year. It goes through a country in which there is a good deal of wood, after that, a fine farming country. Country Harbour is one of the best harbours on the coast. It also goes through a tract of iron which has been taken up by the Whitney Company.

Will the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) tell us whether this road and some others that are being built down in Nova Scotia, will not eventually be linked into a system that will be a rival to the Intercolonial Railway ?

No, it will be a feeder. It will be from New Glasgow and strike the southern coast in the county of Guysborough at Country Harbour. On this 80 miles of road all the products of the country will be taken to New Glasgow to be shipped on the Intercolonial Railway ; it will be a feeder of the Intercolonial Railway.
Why not produce the map ?
Because it was produced before.

I can say in reply to the Minister of Railways and Canals, that for myself I.do not desire to lengthen the proceedings for one minute. But I think we are entitled to have full explanations. The fact that the vote went through last year in a perfunctory sort of way is no reason why it should be permitted to go through this year in the same way. The minister says that the map and papers were placed on the Table last year ; then how much easier it would be to put them on the Table now. It is another parliament that was voting the money, I do not want to

make objections now, I want information. The member for Guysborougb has given us some information: he tells us it started from New Glasgow, which is a railway centre.
I know where that is. I have been down there. But some other members of this House are not familiar with the locality, and when we are voting away a quarter of a million dollars, surely the House is entitled to the information upon which that money is to be voted.
This vote is not to be less than a quarter of a million; but if the road costs $28,100 a mile, then the vote will amount to over half a million dollars. It is a very fair request and a very reasonable request, that the minister should put that map on the Table, so that we may know what kind of country will be opened up by this railway and all particulars regarding it before we pass this very large amount. These items will not go through without full explanations, and the minister will be consulting his own convenience if he would give us this information at once.

I have been trying to get a folder of the Intercolonial Railway, so that I might see by the map where this railway goes, but although I can get the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway folders in the lobby of the House, I cannot get one of our own railway. The very least the Minister of Railways should do is to have a map of the province on the Table.
I did not state that we had a plan of this railway. What I said was that all the plans we had were laid on the Table of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister said differently a few minutes ago.

' Hansard ' will show I did not. I think the hon. member is referring to what the member for Guysborougb said. All the maps and plans we had were put on the Table last year, and they were gone over by the hon. gentleman who then represented York, N.B. (Mr. Foster). I have not got the maps here now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Where are they?

They may be in the office. I would not expect that, session after session, hon. members would ask me to lumber up the records with maps referring to railway bonuses which have already been adopted by the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But this is a new parliament.
This is not a new vote.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I never in my lifetime knew of a Minister of Railways bringing subsidy resolutions to the House without
putting upon the Table, either twenty-four hours before or at the time he moved the resolutions, not only the maps, but the whole correspondence in connection with these subsidies. We have a right to that information.

I do not think that the Minister of Railways can be serious in talking about what was done last session, when he knows that there are a great many new members in this parliament. What value is it to these gentlemen that the minister placed some plans on the Table of the House last year?
It is not customary in parliament to have papers prepared and brought down year after year, in connection with matters which have been disposed of already.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why not ?

I do not know, but it has not been the practice. There are very strong reasons why it would not be necessary. The papers that are brought here are not taken back to the office, and it would be a rather serious matter, in view of the volume of work the officials have to perform now, to ask the department to prepare copies of them again. These are revotes that have already been considered and dealt with by parliament, and the inference is that parliament would not require that that work should be done over again.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister knows perfectly well that subsidies are asked for these railways by piecemeal, and that session after session we are asked to subsidize an extension of the line so that the maps and all the information should be before us again. For my part I have no disposition to obstruct, but we certainly should know the particulars of these railways when we are asked to vote such large sums of money for them. If the minister had consulted his own convenience and the convenience of the House, he would have been armed with all the necessary information. Discussion at this stage of the session is entirely without any profit beyond the fact of endeavouring to get some information which would justify us in voting these subsidies. It may be that the change of location of this line is wholly unjustified, and we certainly should have some information to enable us to decide on its merits intelligently.
The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) stated that some of the money was spent in his county. I would like to ask if this money was voted last session ?
It is a revote of the money voted in 1897, and in 1899 again.
How much of this money is not a revote ?

The whole of it is a revote. I would say to the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Robinson), to the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), and. to the committee, that it is not unreasonable, when the Minister of Railways and Canals asks for a new subsidy, that all the details concerning it should be given. I think the House would expect it, but when a revote is simply asked for, of course the minister is not prepared to go into the same wealth of detail that he would go into if he were asking for an appropriation for the first time.
But, the location of this line is changed.
The vote is simply to serve the same locality. The line is changed in its location a few miles one way or the other, but it is to serve the same locality.	*
It is twenty miles.
No, it is not twenty miles.

Well, it is intended to serve the same locality. Under such circumstances the minister, I think, would naturally presume that parliament would be disposed, as it has been in the past, to sanction the revote unless there was some very good ground to the contrary. The same public reasons apply to these revotes as to the original votes unless there may be somebody that thinks there are good grounds to the contrary. I may remind the hon. member for West Elgin that this subject was discussed previously in former parliaments. It was thought advisable to make this appropriation for a railway to serve a section of the country which is absolutely denuded of railway accommodation. I do not know whether there is any railway at all in the county of Guysborough.
Just about two or three miles at Port Mulberry.

The company is a large one, and I do not know that of all the resolutions that have been proposed there is one which would serve a more useful purpose than this one. It was so considered at the time this vote was originally made. The company which was expected to build the road found itself unable to do so, and a new company has been organized. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) has explained the circumstances, and he has stated that a new company is prepared to go on with the work. Under such circumstances it seems to me that the committee has all the information necessary to enable it to come to a conclusion. This appropriation was last voted two years ago. My hon. friend (Mr. Fraser) has explained the change which has taken place in the location of the line, but the road is to serve the same locality.

The right hon. gentleman knows that the province of Nova Scotia is asking us to aid some seven or eight lines. Some are revotes and some are new votes. I am not complaining of the votes, but I am complaining of the want of information that should be disclosed on a map, placed before the committee. I am not only considering this one case, but there are seven or eight cases from that single province. These votes may be meritorious, but we are not in a position to say whether they are or not, owing to the poverty of the information we have on the subject.

Will the right hon. gentleman lay on the Table of the House the correspondence in reference to the new votes, anyway ? Perhaps it will be laid on the Table when the resolution is moved. We will have no opportunity then of looking at it. We ought to have the correspondence on the Table of the House now.

There is no correspondence about this at all. When the new company was formed to build that road in Nova Scotia, it asked power from the legislature of Nova Scotia to build from New Glasgow instead of Sunnybrae, and application was made to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, before the revote was taken, to change the starting point of the line from New Glasgow in place of from Sunnybrae. The only correspondence is the application I made on behalf of the county and people interested in that road to change the point at which the line started.

What is the principle upon which these votes were to be granted a few years ago ? It seems to emphasize the necessity of the papers that are asked for by several hon. members on this side of the House being brought down. Part of this subsidy was voted in 1897, and the Subsidy Act says :
The subsidies hereinbefore mentioned as to be granted to companies named for that purpose shall, if granted by the Governor in Council, be granted to such companies respectively ; the other subsidies may be granted to such companies as are approved by the Governor in Council as having established to his satisfaction their ability to construct and complete the said railways respectively.
They must by some means or other establish to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council their ability to take up this undertaking and complete it, and if so, there must have been some correspondence either oral or by letter.

This is an authorization to the Governor in Council to enter into a subsidy contract, and before entering into a subsidy contract he must be satisfied of the ability of the company to construct the road.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Yes, and when it applies for it as well. That was the principle

followed when the application for the subsidy was made. A few years ago we went much farther than we do now. At first it was held that every company must show its financial ability to complete the undertaking.
Not when the subsidy was granted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, my knowledge antedates that of the hon. minister on this question. That view was afterwards relaxed, and it was provided that when a company was formed and showed its ability to complete the road it should receive the bonus and not until then. But, the other was the principle that formerly obtained and it was held that when it applied for a subsidy it must satisfy the Governor in Council of its ability to complete the road. There must be some correspondence before the government at that time. We are told that this company is ready to go on now. If this company has been newly organized and is a responsible company and is ready to go on to complete the road, surely there must be some correspondence.
Nothing except the application to change the point of starting from New Glasgow instead of Sunny brae.
I understood the hon. gentleman to represent to the government that the company is prepared to go on and build the road.

I did, and I represented also, to show the bona fides of the company, that the local legislature of Nova Scotia, when giving it power had insisted that it should pay $100,000 to secure the completion of the road.

That makes it all the stronger. It takes it out of the category of the second part, which allows the Governor in Council to arrange that if at some future time a company show its bona fides it shall have the subsidy, but this company is now prepared to go on and that makes it all the stronger because all the information should be in the possession of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals.

I did not think that it was necessary to write all the facts to the minister. I went on behalf of the county and of this company, and explained the matter as I have done now, and the minister accepted the explanation. The minister had the further privilege of seeing Mi-. Fitzpatrick, who is the chief man in the undertaking in Nova Scotia, who told him that he was ready to go on. I think that is all the information that was required. On behalf of the county I brought to the hon. minister a man whose name in Nova Scotia is the synonym, not only of the ability, but of character. I communicated the facts to the hon. minister and asked simpiy that 173
this change should be made in the starting point and nothing else. That was all that was required to be done to get a revote of the subsidy which parliament passed before.
You ask an additional vote of $256,000.
Not a cent except what we got before.
What you got in 1897 had lapsed.
Of course, we would not need to vote it unless it had lapsed.
The conditions were that the railway must be begun within two years, and it was not begun.

There is only a portion of this vote which has actally lapsed; but the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) is astray in this particular. He will see, on reference to this clause, that this is for a line of railway from such a point to such a point. It is not voted to any particular company, but is for the line of railway, and it is open to the Governor in Council to require all the evidence which can reasonably be asked from the company proposing to build, as to its ability to carry the work on. That we intend doing. As my hon. friend from Guysborough has said, I had a call from Mr. Fitzpatrick, who Is a man of high reputation and of means, and has had a great deal of railway experience, and he assured me that before he got his contract he would be able to satisfy me, so that I could satisfy my colleagues, that the work would go on, and that he and the gentlemen associated with him would be fully able to put it through. But we have not required yet that that evidence shall he furnished to us.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Since I heard the remarks by the right hon. First Minister, I have not so much objection to this subsidy as I had, because if this is a revote from the last parliament, I think we are in honour bound to carry it out.
They may have made a mistake.
