If they made a mistake, it was their mistake and not ours; and I think that unless some reason to the contrary can be given, we ought to carry it out. I was thinking, when the hon. member for Guysborough was speaking, that it took Sam Slick a long time to get those Bluenoses warmed up; and when they have only built two miles of railway in the large county he represents, I think it is about time somebody warmed them into a railroad. I do not think it right that the whole country should pay for their railroad, unless they have contributed to other railroads in other sections, as the Finance Minister says they have. I do not wish to talk parish politics, because that has been the talk half



the time in this House, aud I think it is about time we talked of something of more consequence. Not that parish politics is to be despised; but if we are to tell every little incident that has happened in railroad matters in the last fifty years, we may as well go home and tell what we did in our own counties. The people in my county some years ago built a railroad some twenty-three miles in length; they built it themselves. There was no government granting bonuses in those days. When the Canada Southern, which runs through the peninsula from the Detroit river to the Niagara river, was built, the people living in the country through which it ran built it themselves. The county of Elgin gave $225,000, and the townships also gave aid. Now, I am going to move a resolution. Will it be in order, Mr. Chairman ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, it will be in order.

It is as follows:
It is in the opinion of this House that the strictest economy should be exercised throughout all the public service, that subsidies should not be granted to individuals or to enterprises of any kind, unless it can be clearly shown that the whole country will be benefited thereby, and that all subsidies should be brought down during the first week of every session.
I think it is too late to discuss these questions now. I think the people of the country ought to have known that these subsidies were coming up, so that they might have discussed them fully. If the government would carry out, now that they are in power, the same policy they advocated when in opposition, they would not have all these men on this side of the House barking at them and throwing stones at them. This shows how careful we on this side of the House should be as to what we say, because all these things will be brought against us when we get into power. I trust that this government will carry out the policy they advocated, not only in regard to subsidies, but in regard to economy and everything else. If they do, the country will thank them.
Bring your motion up.
Will you second It ?
Yes, I will second it.

Before these resolutions are passed through the committee, I wish to refer to the conditions that go with these subsidies. Before doing so, however, I wish to say that I am totally opposed to the continuance of this policy of subsidizing railroads. Of course, the majority of this House are of the opposite opinion, but in that respect I do not think they are in accord with the feeling of the country. I think the country is ripe for a new policy on the railway question, and I submit that one way to favour a new policy is to do everything we can to demolish the old

system. I am not at all impressed with the force of the argument that we should continue this policy of subsidizing railways, because it has been followed in the past, and we should carry it on until all the outlying districts of the country have been served with railway communication. If that were so, there would be no end to the policy at all. And yet I do not see that that is being carried out, for I notice that in the resolutions the western part of this Dominion is only getting thirty-five miles of railway- the Gimli extension near Lake Winnipeg. It is rather remarkable that this is the same thirty-five miles of railway that was the cause of a new-born zeal in the Railway Committee when the Canadian Pacific Railway asked for a charter for the Toulon line extension. It was then moved in the Railway Committee that that charter should not become operative until the Canadian Pacific Railway had constructed an extension to Gimli. Now, we find that the Canadian Pacific Railway has a further inducement to build that extension by an offer of $112,000.
But the matter I specially wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to is the wage clause. So as not to go into a lot of explanation, I will just quote one paragraph from the speech of the Postmaster General as reported in ' Hansard.' The last act of the last parliament was to pass the current wage resolution, on the 17th July last, the day before prorogation, providing that the fair-wage clause be inserted in all contracts and on works subsidized by the government. The Postmaster General then spoke as follows :
When it receives the sanction of parliament, it is a mandate and authority to the government to incorporate such a condition in government contracts; and, if this House sanctions the resolution, the principle of it will he lived up to by the government. My hon. friend opposite asks why this provision is not Incorporated in the Act respecting subsidies to railways. If they had been as attentive to find out what is in that Act as to assert what is not in it, they would have found that there is a provision to the effect of the granting of these subsidies shall be upon such conditions as may be set forth in the agreement between the government and the railways respecting such subsidies. If this resolution receives the sanction of the House, it will be the duty of the government and the Minister of Railways, representing the government, to incorporate the provisions of this resolution in the agreements relating to railway subsidies, and it will become one of the conditions regulating the right of railways to receive subsidies. This resolution expressly states that the fair wages principle shall apply to all works aided by subsidies of public money. If hon. gentlemen opposite desire this condition to be incorporated in these subsidies, let this resolution receive their approval, and it will become the duty of the government to live up to it in their dealings with the railways.
That resolution did receive the approval of the House, and yet I understand it is not being incorporated in the conditions of these

railway subsidies. I submit that the Minister of Railways should either assure us that the clause will be inserted in these subsidy grants or that he will himself move to revoke the action parliament took last year. I supported this resolution in good faith because I believed the government would make it operative, and I Intend to bring this matter before every parliament until that resolution is either revoked or carried out.
All the contracts which have been entered into for subsidies since last session contain a clause incorporating the fair-wage provision.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am very pleased to hear that, because we were told differently some time before the session.
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. The hon. gentleman has reference to the contract for locomotives, in which that clause was not inserted, but I understand that it is embodied in the contracts now entered into.
Mr.	PUTTEE.	Have any works	been
proceeded with under the subsidies granted since that date.
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	ANDCANALS. Yes, several railways are under construction,	and	the contract	with
those companies contain that clause.

It seems to me that the government have scarcely done, in connection with the vote, all that they should. The policy agreed on in voting these subsidies was that when the government knew that a company was able and prepared to build the road, the subsidy would be voted direct to it. The hon. member for Guysbor-ough has said that there is a live company in operation, which has made a deposit with the local government of $100,000, as evidence of its ability and intention to build the road. If that be the case, it was the duty of the government to vote the subsidy direct to that company, and the government should bring down the correspondence and all the evidence that satisfied it as to the ability and bona fides of the company. The reason why the policy was agreed on that where a company showed its ability and good faith the subsidy should be voted to that company direct, was to prevent the government playing off one company against another and making such bargain as would be satisfactory to them, either with friend or foe. That was the reason advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite for voting a subsidy direct to the company. If that was a good argument then, it is equally good to-day.

What this company has to do is to deposit the $100,000, and both governments must be satisfied that the money is deposited to their credit before they will make the contract. The government is perfectly safe, because the bona fides of the 1731
company must be established before the contract is let. There is no other company that can build this road except this company. It is the only existing corporation that is ready to build it.
Then the subsidy ought to be voted directly to that corporation.
They only got their charter this winter.
The subsidy was voted, in the first instance, in the manner it was, because there was no company then prepared to build the road. The minister now says that the company are only building a portion
I said that the whole subsidy had not lapsed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It has all lapsed except what was voted for the last fifteen miles.
The MiNISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. No.
Yes, what was voted in the Railway Act of 1897 must have lapsed, because the subsidy provided that the road should be begun within two years. That was for 65 miles.
Have you the Act of 1899 there ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: All it says is for a railway not exceeding fifteen miles. That meant fifteen miles in addition to the sixty-five miles. It did not revote the other subsidy, but granted a subsidy for fifteen miles further. All that subsidy has, therefore, lapsed except the fifteen miles, so we are granting the whole subsidy over again, and we are told that there is a company quite prepared and willing to build the road. It ought then to be voted direct to that company, provided the government bring down correspondence and evidence to satisfy us of the ability of the company to carry out the undertaking.

On that point, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) would reconsider his -view as to voting a bonus to a particular company. My own view is that, except where you know that a company is bona fide established in some way
The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) says that this company is.
He says that it is a very reputable company. But it has not built any railways.
That is not necessary.

I think that where a company has received a subsidy and is actually engaged in building a I railway, it is well to continue any grant to I that company. But where that is not the case the purpose may best be served by

granting the subsidy, not to the company, but to the line of railway. The reason is that, if one company fails to carry out the project, you are free to make an arrangement with another without coming back to parliament-and no good purpose is served by coming back to parliament. A number of years ago, when the railway subsidies were first introduced, a subsidy was voted to a particular company for the building of a railway in Nova Scotia. I remember speaking to Sir Charles Tapper about it, and suggesting that it would be better to vote that subsidy to the road, thus leaving him free to give it to any company. As I say, that was the first year of the railway subsidies, and the government had not thought the matter out. The company to whom the subsidy was granted was never able to build the road, but the fact that the subsidy was thus voted created difficulties which for many years were experienced in that part of the country. If it is well to build a railway, under ordinary circumstances, it is best to vote the subsidy for the railway and leave the minister to find a company to build it. As to this road, I think there is not much exception to be taken to it. A few miles this side of New Glasgow, as you come toward Halifax, there is a little branch railway that runs to a place called Sunnybrae. When the people undertook to build the railway now under discussion, they thought it would be well to start from the terminus of the branch at Sunnybrae. But the project was not carried out, and now, the new-comers say that they do not want to run over a branch railway and deal with another company, but rather to run direct to the Intercolonial Railway from New Glasgow. You start from a different point, and a few miles out you reach the common line. Mr. Fitzpatrick, the gentleman who proposes to build this line, is a gentleman of the highest respectability, and I have no reason to doubt that he is well able to carry out what he says. I once heard of a man who was said to be a worthy man, though an Episcopalian. Mr. Fitzpatrick is a worthy man, though a Conservative member of the Nova Scotia legislature. He is a contractor who is believed to have large means, and I would have implicit faith in anything he might say. He told me that he believed that if a subsidy was arranged for, the company could be found to build the road. I do not know whether the Minister of Railways and Canals has had any correspondence with him, but I am sure that if he had a cartload of correspondence he could not add anything material to what has been placed before this House.
Are we to have the correspondence for the new votes ?
I have the original papers here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The statement was made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals Mr. FIELDING.
that when the vote was up before, full information was given, and that it would be work of supererogation to go over the ground a second time. Now, I have taken the trouble to find out what was done when this vote was taken. The first intimation we had of It came in the form of a -question, as follows :

speakeroldname: Sir CHARLES HIBBERT TUPPER (for Mr. Borden, Halifax) asked :
speechtext:
Has the government given any promise or other assurance of a subsidy in aid of the construction of a railway from Sunnybrae, in the county of Pictou, to any and what place in the county of Halifax, or in the county of Guys-borough, in Nova Scotia ?
To which the Minister of Railways and Canals replied as follows :

No action has been taken by government on the application for subsidy in aid of the construction of a railway from Sunnybrae, in the county of Pictou, to any place in the county of Halifax, or in the county of Guysborough.
The next reference to it was after midnight on June 28th-or rather June 29th. This was the last day of the session, except that the House sat on June 29th, which was the day of prorogation, for one hour, from eleven to twelve o'clock, noon. When this matter was brought up it was after one o'clock in the morning, as was shown by the fact that shortly before Mr. Foster had said :
* It is now one o'clock, and I suppose we are not going to be kept here any longer.' There was a wordy warfare whether the House should continue sitting, as all the members were tired out, and it was thought that the House should adjourn. The Minister of Railways proposed an item :
For a railway from Sunnybrae to Country Harbour and thence to Guysborough, in the province of Nova Scotia, a distance of sixty-five miles.
The whole explanation given by the Minister of Railways is contained in six lines of ' Hansard,' as follows :
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. Mr. Blair).

speechtext:
We propose to make a slight alteration. I move to strike out the words ' and thence,' which are in the first line, and insert the words, * from a point at or near the Country Harbour cross-road.'
The Minister has told the House that he had plans and correspondence on the Table at that time, that all the papers were before the House and that there was ample time for consideration. This was the last day of the session, even the very last hour, for, in the hour from eleven to twelve on the day of prorogation, very little business could be done, as hon. members could easily understand. But, in answer to a question from Mr. Foster, * What will be the total length ? ' the hon. member for Guysborough said :
The road will be a few miles longer than sixty-five.
