A survey has been made from Sunnybrae to Country Harbour. A subsidy was granted from the Intercolonial Railway to Sunnybrae by the late government, and also for five miles now to be built. A company has offered to build this road to Country Harbour, which is a very important harbour on the southern shore of Nova Scotia, with a branch from Country Harbour cross-road to Guysborough.
Resolution, as amended, agreed to.
That is the whole debate ; there is all the information given to the House when this question first came up. And I say that is not the full and ample information that we want and that we are entitled to receive. To say that this is a, revote and that ample information was given before is not in accordance with our own records ; and I think we can fairly ask the minister, without laying ourselves open to the taunt of obstruction, to give us full information, to place the map on the Table for the benefit of those who have no personal knowledge of the district, so that we may understand what we are voting.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I explained the idea, but hon. gentlemen opposite were quite ready to vote the subsidy. I have the map here and shall be glad to give all the facts to the hon. gentlemen.
I shall be glad to see the map. That is one of the things we have been waiting for.

At the time the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) speaks of, the hon. gentlemen on his side were quite satisfied with the bona fides of the company, and were glad to vote the subsidy, because I asked for it.
I shall be glad to look at the map. We are within our duty as members of parliament in asking for this information, and we are going to have it.

It is painful to observe the position that our hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and even our good friend the First Minister, occupy here this afternoon, after the speeches they made in this House in years gone by against the best interests of this country, and which have been quoted to them to-day. I must say, and I say it after deliberation, that they did not pursue a policy that was in the best interests of Canada. Notwithstanding the speeches that were made in past years on the left of the Speaker by the McMullens and men of that stripe, decrying the policy that was laid down by the late Sir John A. Macdonald for the upbuilding of this country, I say that if this country is prosperous to-day it is due to the fact that the Liberal-Conservative party, both when in power and in opposition, have pursued and endorsed the policy that is now being pursued by the present government in bonus-ing railways. I trust that as long as the
Liberal-Conservative party is in power we will never be burdened by men of the McMullen stripe, who will get up in this House and deliver speeches directly contrary to their former policy, such as was delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few minutes ago. The policy followed by the Liberal-Conservative party with respect to the bonusing of railways was this : That bonuses for railways built for the purpose of opening up new districts in a province, opening up territories within the jurisdiction of a province, should come from the provinces ; but, that bonuses for railways opening up territories and districts under the jurisdiction of the Dominion should come from the Dominion. Later on they changed that policy of bonusing only through lines and great lines of trade, to bonusing to a large extent local lines. I do not think that any hon. gentleman on the Liberal-Conservative side is authorized to stand up in this House and oppose the bonusing of railways. No man authorized to speak for this party has yet declared formally against the policy of bonusing railways in every part of the Dominion of Canada for the purpose of opening up the country. So far as I am concerned, I shall not follow the lead of any man who lays down such a policy as that. Now, what are the facts in regard to the granting of bonuses ? It is true that when our party was in power we pursued the same shilly-shallying policy that the Minister of Railways and Canals Is pursuing now, bringing down these votes without having sufficient information to place on the Table of the House. The railway subsidies were always left till the last days of the session. Our friends in opposition condemned that, and pledged themselves that if they attained to power, in case they should not abolish entirely the bonusing of railways, they would at least pursue a different policy. They have failed to do so, and, therefore, are censurable for failing to carry out their pledges. We have heard a good deal about the benefits of the Parry Sound branch of the Canada Atlantic Railway. The men who built up that road are largely the same men who are applying for the grant that is now under discussion, men who have been successful railway contractors, and who, at the present time, are at work on a large contract in Nova Scotia. I can see no objection to this bonus, nor to any other bonus that I find on the list; and unless some facts are disclosed other than those now before us, I shall support every bonus that is proposed here to-day.

I desire to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals if he is in possession of any information as to whether any portion of this railway, including such bridges as are provided for, is likely to exceed a cost of $15,000 per mile ?

I have been over the section of

country several times, and it is not a difficult line of railway to construct. 1 do not know any reason why it should cost over $15,000 per mile. There will be a couple of bridges, but they will not be expensive bridges. We could scarcely expect to have any plan or survey of the road before the company has got fairly on its feet. Still, my impression is that $15,000 per mile would more than cover the cost of this railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Notwithstanding what has been said by the hon. member for Victoria, I must say, for myself, as a member of the Conservative party, that I am not in favour of the wholesale bonusing of railways, as we have been doing year after year. I believe the sentiment of the country is against it. While saying that, I admit there are exceptional instances where It is justifiable. Where a railway is going into a new country, and which would not be likely to be built unless a substantial bonus was given-in that case it may be justifiable to subsidize a railway. Why should we not take a lesson from what is being done in the United States for several years past, where they loan money for building railways ? The Minister of Railways and Canals says it is difficult to get proper security. But, what they have done we can do. It is only a few years ago since the Union Pacific Railway was obliged to pay back $25,000,000 of money loaned to build that road. I can go into the library and find a dozen other similar cases. If they are able to get security, why not we ? They are building railways through a country similar to ours. Therefore, I say the time has passed when we should be constantly giving subsidies to railways, the consequence of which is usually to make millionaires or wealthy corporations, rather than doing good to the locality. It has become the practice of railway corporators to lay out their plans to make a raid on parliament year after year to get as many of these railway subsidies as they can. Before we adjourned at one o'clock, the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) attacked some remarks I had made when I drew attention to the fact that the Reform party, if they were honest, ought to drop this policy of railway subsidies. When I referred to the fact that a leading member of the Reform party had written a letter against it, the hon. member for Annapolis replied: We are not to be bound by the ipse dixit of every man who belonged to the Reform party. The Minister of Trade and Commerce wrote an important letter, which appeared in the Farmers' Sun, in order to influence that large class of people known as the Patrons, at that time. I have that letter before me, it is headed ' Like unto like must be alike.' This is the heading that, I presume, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce put upon it. What does he say ?
Read it all.

I will not read it all, because I do not wish to retard the debate. He says :
I know, no man better, how utterly fatal any protective system must be.
He then goes on to speak of that. He afterwards says :
Our policy and platform are exactly the same as yours.
Further he says :
What are the other planks of the Patron platform affecting Dominion politics ? They are these: 1. Economy of administration. 2. Purity and independence of parliament. 3. Tariff for revenue only. 4. Reciprocal trade. 5. Protection of labour from monopolies. 6. No railway bonuses.
And so on. He says further :
You see, as I have said, that the objects of both organizations are absolutely identical. The Liberal party for fifteen years and more have been fighting at heavy odds for the very objects the Patrons profess to desire. The Liberal party lost office rather than forsake these principles.
So he goes on all through that letter saying that the Liberal platform is exactly the same as that of the Patrons, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) says that we are not to have regard to what is said by a prominent member of the Reform party.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ?
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) only wants to ask me a question, I have no objection, but I should prefer to go on and finish what I have to say.
If the hon. gentleman does not want me to interrupt him, I will wait until he is finished.

What I was going to say is that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) reminded this committee that the Reform party laid down its platform in 1893 and that it was bound by that platform, but this letter was written on October 24, 1894, as an addenda to the platform laid down in 1893 and written by the oldest member of the Reform party in Ontario, a man who was the leader of the Reform party in Ontario, the mouthpiece of the party, and whose utterances are entitled to be regarded as the utterances of the party. On the eve of the general election this letter was written for the purposes of the election by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, declaring that his party was in harmony with the Patrons in regard to subsidies to railways, but, he sits in this House today and has not a word to say against railway subsidies. He swallows his words and his friends say that we are not to pay any attention to his utterances because they are the utterances of an insignificant member of the party.

May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) if he has not, himself*

during tlie present session, promoted a railway subsidy and urged the granting of it on the government ?
Which ?
A railway subsidy.
State your case.

I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) if he has not, himself, during the present session, urged the granting of a railway subsidy upon the government ?
Mr. SPROuLE. 1 do not know what the hon. member (Mr. Wade) is referring to.
I am asking the hon. gentleman a simple question. Has he not endeavoured to have a railway subsidy granted to a railway by the government ?

I will answer the hon. gentleman if he sits down, and I will say what I have already said. I< regarded the railway that was applying to the government for a subsidy as an exceptional one. and I urged the granting of a subsidy. I have said more than twice here to-day that I am not opposed to all of these subsidies, I [DOT]am not saying that I am opposing all of these subsidies ; I am only drawing attention to the inconsistency of a party in their wholesale defence of subsidies now, whereas a few years ago they condemned the granting of subsidies.	.
The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has placed words in my mouth that I never uttered. I would be pleased if he would retract them.
What words ?
That I was supporting wholesale subsidies to railways.
I did not say that.
Yes, X understood the hon. member to say that I had said that I did not regard any member of a party as speaking for him when he opposed railway subsidies, because I was in favour of them.
In favour of the principle.
I understood the hon. gentleman to refer to all those subsidies that are on the list. They are not wholesale subsidies, even if he likes to call them so.
I am willing to accept that; X have nothing to retract.

I just rose to give the hon. gentleman an opportunity of putting himself on record. I stand here to support the principle, and to support any party that supports the principle of judicious bonusing of railways and canals and to oppose any party that opposes the principle of bonuses to railways and also canals. I want to say that I think that a good deal
of the attack that has been made is very proper owing to the outrageous conduct in the past of hon. gentlemen occupying positions on the Treasury benches. I think this line of attack is justified, and, so far as I am concerned, there will be no possibility in the future of the Liberal-Conservative party being put in the same box by our opponents being able to quote speeches we have made against the best interests of the country to the same extent as has been done with this statement of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce here to-day. What is the principle at the root of the bonusing of railways and why are these selections made ? Is any hon. member of this House able to stand up in his place and point out an instance where a bonus was given to a road that was not in the interest of the country ? There have been bonuses granted which were never carried out, but if the railways for which these bonuses were granted had been constructed the country would have been the gainer. The district which I have the honour to represent Aas not received any Dominion government bonuses, but the people of that locality have taxed themselves in enormous sums for the building of railways. The people of that locality have burdened themselves by this tax without getting competition between railways, because the roads that they bonused were amalgamated with other railways and they lost the competition. I maintain that these people living in a locality where no federal government railway subsidies were given at all, are entitled to the consideration of the people of this country, possibly not in a way of repaying the bonuses, but at all events, in some way. A railroad in a district benefits the nation as much as the company that constructs it. There is a great deal of opposition to these bonuses because half a dozen railway men have succeeded where hundreds have failed. We have hundreds of men up and down the country who have lost their property, their wealth and the wealth of others, who have undertaken railway construction. Some half dozen men have been able to succeed and are in a position possibly to carry out the enterprises with which they have become associated, but there are hundreds who are unsuccessful. The mere fact that these men have succeeded and that others have failed by hundreds is no reason why the principle of bonusing should not be continued. I maintain that the country gets value even if none of these safeguards were required. The country gets full value in the opening up of new territories, in securing competition, and in various other ways for all the money it gives, just as well as the company does. The principle of bonusing judicious schemes-and whoever heard of a wildcat scheme being bonused, certainly not I, and I have been in the House for ten years-the principle of bonusing judicious railway schemes is a good one for the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite opposed it in

the past, but I am sure they are heartily ashamed of their past conduct now. If when their speeches were quoted against them to-day these gentlemen could be photographed, their faces would resemble the patent medicine advertisement ' before taking ' and ' after taking.' I trust no policy will be laid down by any party in this House against the judicious bonusing of railways for the opening up of the country.

We are now in the closing days of the session, and gentlemen on this side of the House have fairly stated their position and shown up the inconsistency of the government in their policy on this matter. Gentlemen on this side find fault because plans and correspondence have not been brought down. I understand that we are dealing with the first resolution here, and if the member for Guysborough is correct in the information he gave, I see no reason why this resolution should not pass, and pass now. He tells us that the minister has no correspondence in connection with this matter, and if that be true the minister cannot lay any correspondence on the Table. We have been shown a map, and if that map is correct, then I think that the electoral district of Guysborough is entitled to this railway. I, for one, will support this resolution, on the understanding given by the hon. gentleman from Guysborough. Now, at this late state of the session, after the case has been once stated, and stated plainly, surely it is not necessary to repeat these statements oyer and over again. I cannot see that it will do any particular good, and I think we have already wasted sufficient time without wasting any more.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) has moved a resolution which, not being relevant to the resolution under discussion, is out of order. I find on page 552 of Bourinot :
It is irregular to discuss any motion in committee which is not relevant to the resolution under consideration. It is also out of order to move the adoption of a general resolution with respect to any particular vote.
1,	therefore, rule this resolution of the hon. member (Mr. Robinson) out of order. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt this resolution No. 1.
Carried.

Resolution agreed to.
2.	To the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company, for a line of railway from a point at or near ChaudiSre Junction on the Grand Trunk Railway, Quebec, towards the present terminus of the St. Francis branch of the Temis-couata Railway, New Brunswick, not exceeding forty-five miles, and for a line of railway from the mouth of the St. Francis river, New Brunswick, westerly towards ChaudiSre Junction, not exceeding fifteen miles, in lieu of the subsidy granted by 1900, chap. 8, sec. 2, p^yagraph 23; also for a line of railway in extension of the
St. Francis branch of the Temiscouata Railway to the mouth of the St. Francis river. New Brunswick, in lieu of the subsidy granted by 1899, chap. 7, sec. 2, paragraph 43, not exceeding three miles; in all not exceeding sixty-three miles, $201,600.

This resolution amends in one particular the Act passed last session with respect to this railway. This is a railway which is projected for the purpose of connecting with some point on the Intercolonial Railway, either Chaudiere or St. Charles Junction, and running back in the rear portion of the country, which borders on the American line, giving railway connection to the people of that district who are now excluded from railway advantages by reason of their distance from the road along the St. Lawrence and the high ground which intervenes. We now ask that the junction which was fixed at St. Charles Junction may be varied to the Chaudi6re Junction. The second clause provides for the revival of the subsidy for three miles of railway which was granted in 1899, for the purpose of connecting that line with what may be called a branch of the Temiscouata Railway, at the mouth of the St. Francis river. Three miles intervene there which require to have a railway, and a subsidy was granted two years ago for that purpose. It has not been constructed, but we are assured by the hon. minister who represents that county that the line will be built if the subsidy be renewed, and we are asking parliament to revive the subsidy for these three miles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not understand the hon. minister about the connection.
An extension of the St. Francis branch of the Temiscouata Railway, three miles to the mouth of the St. Francis.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I thought that had already been built.
I wish to ask the Minister of Railways what were the reasons given for the alteration of the conditions of the subsidy voted last year ? Under this resolution this line will strike a different point.

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Talbot) that the reason which was given, as set forth by the member for Victoria (Mr. Costigan), is that the object of the company is to make connection with the Quebec bridge.
Will not this railway make a shorter route into New Brunswick than the Intercolonial Railway ?
That is the expectation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then you are bonusing a road for private individuals that will be a shorter route than the Intercolonial Railway.

Don't you think that in the public interest this should be made a part of the Intercolonial Railway rather than that we should bonus a rival company, and place them at a considerable advantage over ns ?
How much shorter will the line be, as now proposed, compared with the line subsidized last session ?

I do not know that this line would be any shorter. I do not think the change has been for the purpose of shortening the route, but as I understand it, the object of the promoters of this railway is to bring their Tine directly to the Quebec bridge, which is now being constructed. That is the object which is put before the government, and that is the object which it is intended to serve by this resolution. My bon. friend (Mr. Talbot) knows the locality better than I do.
I would like to have my question answered. Are we voting this money to make a shorter route that will rival the Intercolonial Railway ?

We are voting it to open a section of the country of great value, which is absolutely without any railway connection at present. It so happens that the railroad which will serve this section of the country will also be the shortest route between Quebec and St. John, N.B. That is a very good reason, perhaps, for making it a government road, but I must say to my hon. friend that the government is not prepared at this moment to adopt his policy and construct more government roads.

Then I take it that the declaration is made by the Prime Minister that he is ready to commit suicide-to kill the government road. This is his confession. He puts himself and his party in this position, that while they are custodians of that great property owned by the whole Dominion, they are going, for some local interest, to cut its throat. I am ashamed to hear such a confession as this made in this House. I have long had my eye on this mode of strengthening the government railway. I spent last week going down and looking over the whole situation. I have heard declarations in this House that the country must do something to solve the transportation problem, and it has been said that these bonuses which are being voted to-day are steps in the solution of that problem. They are nothing of the kind; they only aggravate the conditions which prevent a proper solution; and here is the government of the day proposing to open up a new road that will be a rival of the government road, and will tend to prevent a proper solution of the transportation problem. My idea of the solution of that problem is not the bonusing of every railway that comes along ; but there must be a railroad owned and controlled by the government of Canada from the Georgian Bay
to the city of Quebec, and thence to an ocean winter port in New Brunswick or Nova Scotia. That road must be a first-class road in every respect. If I gained any information at all by the journey of last Saturday and Sunday, it was this, that there must be a great wheat road between the Georgian Bay and the seaboard, and that that road must go as far to the north as possible. To my mind it lies along the route of the Parry Sound road to the Ottawa river crossing at Hawkesbury, and thence by the straightest route to the city of Quebec. The road which we passed over last Sunday is not, I am sorry to say, what you would call a wheat road, owing to its sharp curves and steep grades. A wheat road must be as nearly on the level as possible. The mere building of what are called colonization roads will never solve the transportation problem. We must have a road from the Georgian Bay, as straight as we can get it, to the city of Quebec ; and then, for winter transportation, a road from the city of Quebec through Canadian territory by the most direct route to St. John or Halifax or Sydney, or wherever the port may be. I have long had my eye on the proposition to get a short cut from the city of Quebec via the Temiscouata Railway, if it can be got on reasonable terms, or by some other line, to the city of St. John ; and now we are proposing to subsidize a railway which we shall have to acquire shortly for that very purpose. While on my feet I want to refer to another phase of the transportation question which I gathered on that trip last week. The largest river and lake boats can meet the largest ocean steamers at the port of Quebec to-day. The water side of the transportation problem is now in a very fair shape, especially as the lower portion of the St. Lawrence is to be lighted properly, as the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries told us the other day ; but we have not done a single thing yet to solve the rail side of the problem. The Grand Trunk have come the nearest to it by the way they run their Midland line to Montreal, and in a short time they will be devoting their energy to improving that road and giving it the best possible grades. But Quebec to-day is in a position, without any further expenditure, to handle millions of bushels of grain ; I do not believe Montreal is in that position ; and the Grand Trunk Railway have come to the point that they intend to be in the race for the carrying of the wheat that is to be carried by rail, .and they intend to spend more money in reducing their grades and getting the best possible line from Midland to Montreal or Quebec, or wherever their port may be. Now, the government are the custodians of the Intercolonial Railway, and they must find a way of supplying the links on that railway so that it will become a competitor or a rival, or, if you like to put it so, an

assistant of the Grand Trunk in doing the transportation by rail.
Would not the Canadian Pacific Railway own the bulk of this line between Temiscouata and St. John ?

They might or might not. If the Canadian Pacific Railway get it, then so much the worse for the Intercolonial Railway. But the real rail solution of the problem is in getting the most direct line between the Georgian Bay via Quebec to St. John or Halifax, and this bonus is against that object. Just one word more in regard to that visit to Quebec of last week, and in regard to a Bill which will be presented here in connection with the transportation question. A proposal will be made to parliament to give to the Quebec Terminal Railway control of the entrance to Quebec along the Champlain road. I want to point out to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways that if ever Quebec is to be the ocean port of Canada, as I believe it will be for nine or ten months of the year, the entrance to the harbour will be along Champlain street.
Not from the west.

It will be for the great wheat road that will cross the Ottawa at Hawkesbury. If the hon. gentleman thinks he can get down by the St. Charles valley, he will make a mistake. The only way to get down to the harbour, where you can meet the large ocean liners, is along Champlain street ; and that little narrow entrance to the great harbour of Canada should not' be allowed to pass Into the hands of a private corporation. I protest against the Minister of Railways coming down here with a bonus which is aimed at the usefulness of the Intercolonial Railway owned by the people, and which will create a rival system to the national system.

With regard to the relation of this Quebec and New Brunswick Railway to the Intercolonial, I think my hon. friend who has just taken his seat is somewhat mistaken. It is several miles away from the Intercolonial Railway, and is some distance from Quebec. The chef-lieu of my county is about twenty-five miles from Quebec. This new railway is already fifteen miles from the Intercolonial and keeps going further to the boundary of Maine all the time until it strikes the back of the county of Kamouraska. It would not affect the traffic of the Intercolonial Railway in any way.
Will it not make a shorter system ?

It will be a shorter route to St. John. It will be much shorter than either the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Intercolonial Railway from the city of Que-Mr. MACLEAN.
bee. The railway will run through a portion of country along the United States border, which has no railway communication and never had any. The Grand Trunk Railway formerly stopped at Riviere du Loup, but subsequently, the government purchased the Riviere du Loup branch, running along the water front of the St. Lawrence to L6vis ; but, in that portion of the country which this road is to traverse, and which is unprovided with railway communication, there are magnificent parishes all the way, thirty to seventy-five miles back of the St. Lawrence, while the Intercolonial Railway ruris along at a distance of only three or four miles from the St. Lawrence. Petitions have been sent to parliament for years asking for the construction of this Quebec and New Brunswick line, and there can be no doubt that it will contribute largely to the development of that back country.
The only objection that I now raise is to the change in the wording of the subsidy. When this road was first subsidized, it was agreed to construct it to a point on the Intercolonial Railway at St. Charles Junction, now we are asked to construct it to Chaudiere Junction, but whether it strikes either point will not shorten the line in any way or affect the traffic from the west.
I insist on the subsidy being left as it was originally voted, because the road would then go to a point in my county whicii is not provided with a railway, whereas by the *change it will go to St. Anselme. which already has railway connection, and because, in either case, as I have said, the line will not be shortened and the traffic from the west not affected.
There is already a road, the old Grand Trunk Rivifere du Loup branch, which runs from Levis by way of Chaudiere down to St. Charles, and by striking a point on the Intercolonial Railway at St. Charles Junction, you then utilize the old portion of the Intercolonial from St. Charles to the Chaudiere, and make it not merely a freight road but also a freight and passenger road. That is why I insist that the wording of the old subsidy should not be changed. There is no advantage in changing the wording, as that will not in any way shorten the line or help it in its traffic arrangements. I insist upon our going back to the wording of the old subsidy, because we will then give the old road the importance which it has lost since the building of the new St. Charles branch. If this new road strikes the Intercolonial Railway at a point at or near St. Charles Junction, it will give the old portion of the road three or four times the value it now has as a freight or passenger carrier.
Is the road, as proposed in this subsidy, to cross the Quebec bridge ?
Yes.
Will not that road have a union or some station connected with the Intercolonial Railway ?
I think that the intention of the new road is to connect with the Great Northern at the St. Lawrence bridge.

My hon. friend, who is familiar with the locality, knows where the ChaudiSre Junction is. It is intended that the St. Lawrence bridge will connect with the ChaudiSre Junction, and the object of the amendment is to bring this Quebec and New Brunswick road direct to Chaudiere Junction, so as to give it immediate access to the Quebec bridge.
It will have some connections all the same with the Intercolonial at the Chaudiere.

This is just another illustration of the outrage on the rights of this House, that we have nothing to show where this road runs. The hon. Minister of Railways has plenty of draughtsmen at his command and they could easily furnish us with the maps required.
They have more now than they can do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Surely, the House is entitled to some consideration. It is an outrage upon our rights that we should be asked to vote these subsidies blindly, without knowledge of the localities.
We are trying to find out. on the map where the road is which we are subsidizing, and are unable to do it.

1 think I can satisfy the hon. gentleman. My hon. friend could not have a better map of the province of Quebec or New Brunswick than he has in his head. This railway is intended to start in the neighbourhood of Chaudiere Junction, then to 'go behind the chain of mountains and strike the valley of St. John river, and then strike the system of the New Brunswick Railways. My hon. friend knows that there is a chain of mountains at a short distance from the St. Lawrence, and the colonization movement has crossed the mountain chain and extend on the south side. This road will pass from ChaudiSre Junction to the county of Dorchester, and then follow the counties of Bellechasse, L'lslet. Kamouraska and Temiscouata, until it reaches the valley of the St. John, behind the county of L'lslet.
Near Edmonton.
Edmonton is due south of Riviere du Loup, or thereabouts. It will strike the valley of the St. John perhaps behind the county of L'lslet. My hon. friend knows the locality without referring to a map.
The right hon. gentleman has given us some further and definite information which I am sorry I could not just follow.

This will be another through Canadian Pacific Railway line, and when the new bridge is completed at Quebec, the Canadian Pacific Railway will then be able to use its line on the north shore in connection with this line, as an additional through road to the sea. Some two months ago, I had a motion on the Order paper in favour of reducing the grades on the Intercolonial, to a minimum and giving all railways connecting with that road running powers over it, in order that our seaports might be built up. I also favoured the double-tracking of the line from Moncton to the seaboard, because the more traffic we can bring to our Canadian seaboard, the more will we build up our country.
I move that the words of the subsidy as voted last year be reinstated here.

which it was to pass. We found it almost absolutely necessary, in order to make progress with the construction of the road, that the subsidy , should be available for Clmudiere Junction, because it was the desire of the company to make this connection in order to go over the bridge into the city. Every one will understand the advantage of that to the road, and every one will understand the advantage to the city of having the road reach the city. Therefore, it is not a question of depriving the company of a subsidy, but of throwing the subsidy back into the old form and thus depriving the company of the advantage of reaching Quebec, which would greatly add to the difficulties of carrying out the enterprise. The amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) is a natural one. He represents the county of Bellechasse, and, perhajis from his point of view it is well to force the company to construct to St. Charles Junction. But I wish to call attention to one or two facts. The whole length of this road is calculated at one hundred and thirty odd miles. Over one hundred and ten miles of it would be in the province of Quebec, and not more than eighteen miles in the province of New Brunswick. The legislature of New Brunswick last session, though with limited means, did not hesitate to vote a subsidy for that portion of the road within the province. Some years ago the Quebec legislature granted a charter over the very country over which it is proposed to build now, and voted a bonus of 10,000 acres per mile to encourage the construction of the road. But as this was viewed as a purely colonization road, no capitalists could be found to take hold of it. The subsidy expired. And so the matter remained until a movement was made by the people of our province, and a proposition made to our friends in Quebec, showing that this woidd be an important road and that if we made the connection it would become an interprovincial railway. It was then the gentlemen from the province of Quebec took an active part, and the charter was secured and the subsidy granted. Now, with regard to this three miles, I would like the attention of the exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) for a moment while I explain. The subsidy for that three miles was voted a year before this charter was obtained, and the subsidy granted to this road. It was voted on the old understanding. When the St. Francis was built, it was built as an extension of the Temiscouata and built by the Temiscouata Company. At that time, it was to be built to the mouth of the St. Francis. A subsidy was granted by the government, of which both the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and I were members. AVhen the railway reached Connor station which is the terminus of the branch-
How long is that ?

Thirty-five miles. When the road reached there Mr. Connor had his mills there instead of putting them at the mouth of the St. Francis where we supposed the mills would be. So, it was thought unnecessai'y to push on over the three miles, as there was but little settlement, and no mills to create traffic. Until the mills were established at the mouth of the St. Francis, it was not thought necessary to go on.
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals was speaking of this as being a connecting link of the Temiscouata.

It is the extension of the St. Francis branch of the Temiscouata line. The three miles are covered by the present charter. It is to give the company the benefit of the power to use a subsidy for the three miles voted before that this revote for the three miles is proposed.

The changes I am now asking for do not affect the road in any way. I do not desire to keep the road from going straight to the proposed bridge on the St. Lawrence. It is only to change the route and enable the company to utilize a portion of the Intercolonial Railway which, if the road is built as my hon. friend is asking, will become perfectly useless. Both routes strike the same point, the Quebec bridge. But I want this old portion of the Intercolonial Railway to St. Charles, which is now only used for freight, to be used as a through line for both freight and passengers. The change would not affect the object of the road in any shape or form.

As there is a difference of opinion between the hon. gentlemen who are interested in this road and the proposition to restore the original words of the subsidy, it occurred to me that a modus vivendi might be reached to harmonize the views of both of these hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the subject. I would suggest that the words 'at or near the St. Charles Junction or at or near the Chaudi&re Junction' might be incorporated, so that it would be open to the Governor General in Council to determine which of these points should be made the terminus. It is not a point of great public interest, but if my hon. friend would approve of these words, I would suggest that they be inserted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would be sorry to have any misunderstanding with any Quebec member with regard to this road, as none of them is more interested in it than I am. I would be quite willing to accept the suggestion made, and it would be in keeping with our charter. That would go a little further and give the subsidy, in the wording of the charter itself, to a road from the St. Charles Junction or from the ChaudiSre

Junction, or from a point on the Quebec Central. That would be In accordance with the power parliament has granted to make these connections.

The House seems much concerned in settling a little difference between two rival parishes interested in this railway, but we have not had any statement from the Minister of Railways and Canals in answer to my statement that the shortest line through Canadian territory is being subsidized by the Dominion, and a line that will cut the throat of the Intercolonial Railway as regards traffic. I make that statement here to-day and the government have no answer. I would like to know from the Minister of Railways and Canals what answer he can give, after all the expenditure he is asking the country to make in connection with the Intercolonial Railway-millions of dollars for cars, the contracts have gone through this session-mil-ions of dollars for harbour works at L6vis, in St. John, contracts of all kinds right and left-heavy rails being brought into the country-locomotives being built for a national railway, while a proposition is made here to-day to divert all that traffic from the Intercolonial Railway to a rival scheme owned by private individuals. I am raising a national question, and I would like an answer from the government. We have had the confession of the Prime Minister that this is the short road, and I believe it is the short road, following the line that was originally laid down for the Intercolonial Railway, but which the Imperial authorities objected to and compelled the Intercolonial Railway to take a great round sweep through a very inhospitable country.
The hon. member is altogether mistaken. It was the very best portion of Quebec that was chosen, not a roundabout route. It was no back country then, it was all front country.

The front was taken to keep it as far away as possible from the state of Maine. Now we are coming back to find that the nearest and best line for the Canadian Pacific Railway is as near as we can get to it, and at great expense we are building a southern road there. The same thing is being done with this road and some others. I call the attention of the maritime members to the fact that when we are spending so much money on the Intercolonial Railway in every direction, we are subsidizing a road or a series of little roads, which will be linked into one and which will be made a rival of the Intercolonial Railway, and which stands now to pass into the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway. As one who thinks the Intercolonial Railway is the greatest single asset that Canada possesses to-day. I protest against this. I want the Intercolonial Railway to be kept for the people of Canada as a great road that will be regulative of the Grand Trunk Railway and of the Canadian Pacific Railway. But *
if you are going to build roads that will pass into the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway and of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that will divert the traffic that the Intercolonial Railway has to-day, and its prospective traffic, then you are making a mistake, you are guilty of an unnational policy. It is contrary to the interests of the people of Canada, who are blindly groping to find a solution of what is called the transportation problem. It is simply throwing money away, it is injuring our national interests, and where it is going to end God only knows.

While it is important that nothing should be done to interfere with the Intercolonial Railway, yet it is still more important that we should find the shortest means of communication to the west and the seaboard. It seems to me that is being done by the proposition before us, and therefore I am heartily in favour of it.

I desire to reassure my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) as to the possible disastrous consequences which he apprehends will follow the construction of this line. If this line is built it is not going to be a competitor of the Intercolonial Railway, it is not going to strike a blow at the pre-eminence of that railway in any degree.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How much nearer will St. John be by this road than by Quebec ?

My hon. friend does not realize that the Canadian Pacific Railway would be the owner of this line, at least to the extent of two-thirds if not three-fourths of its entire distance. The Canadian Pacific Railway is the owner of a line from St. John to Montreal through its entire distance, and I cannot conceive the early possibility of the Canadian Pacific Railway acquiring this line or making connections with it, using the rest of its line from Edmonton to St. John, and thereby constituting a through line of railway from Quebec to this point, when the Canadian Pacific Railway has, from another and a further point, a direct line only 440 miles in length from Montreal to St. John.
I am glad to see that the hon. gentleman is a zealous admirer and supporter of the Intercolonial Railway ; I am glad to know that he is solicitous about it at all times and seasons. Solicitous and all as he is, and solicitous as I would naturally be in relation to anything that would be harmful to the Intercolonial Railway, I would not hesitate to give support and assistance to this project, and in doing so I would not feel that it was impinging in the slightest degree on the interests of the Intercolonial Railway. These people have no railway communication. They have a very fine country, as I understand it, and they ought to have railway communication. They have been left practically out in the woods. Why should

we refuse to give them the ordinary aid, traversing a splendid country as this railway does, because we might interfere with the local traffic which would be taken up and which might be diverted from the Intercolonial Railway ? I think there would be no reason to suppose that any traffic as a consequence would fail to be carried by the Intercolonial Railway. I propose that the clause be altered by including all three points which are named in the company's charter at which the construction of this line may commence. X move :
That the words, ' from a point at or near St. Charles Junction, or at or near ChaudiSre Junction, or a point on the Quebec Central Railway, near St. Anselme, Quebec,' be inserted in place of the words ' at or near Chaudidre Junction.'
Resolution as amended, agreed to.
To the Montreal and Province Line Railway Company, for a line of railway from Parnham, Quebec, to Frelighsburg, in lieu of the subsidy granted by 1900, chap 8, sec. 2, paragraph 37, not exceeding nineteen miles, $60,800.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This is a railway that was subsidized last year from Frelighsburg to the international boundary line. It is part of the Montreal and Province line. It has had different names and it lias been six or seven times before parliament, although we subsidized an additional mileage to that which we are now proposing to subsidize. Last year, when we were proposing to subsidize the line from Farnham to the international boundary, the expectation was that the Grand Trunk Railway, either through its main line or the Central Vermont organization, would build the line. The Grand Trunk Railway engaged to build the line, but it concluded that there was no object to be gained by going to the international boundary. The main object was to get to Frelighsburg. The company, in the opinion of the law department of the government, cannot contract to build the line to Frelighsburg under the vote, but they must contract for it to the international boundary, and as it would then only have to take off two miles to reach Frelighsburg, we propose to limit the road to nineteen miles, which will bring it to Frelighsburg.
For a line of railway from a point on the Intercolonial Railway at or near Windsor Junction to Upper Musquodoboit, in lieu of 1897, chap. 4, sec. 2, paragraph 23, not exceeding forty miles, $128,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This is a line of railway connecting the Musquodoboit Valley, a very productive portion of the province of Nova Scotia, with the Intercolonial Railway.
What do you call it ?
Musquodoboit. In that country they have these delightful Indian names.
Are there any -voters along the line ?
There are voters along the line, and I do not mind telling my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) that they are the best type of voters in the world.

I think the subsidy which it is proposed to vote for this line is a very deserving one. It is a curious thing that the county of Halifax has only about twenty-five or thirty miles of railway in it. Although I think there are about 35,000 people in that county, they have been cut off from railway communication at all times. They have not had any railway communication with the outside world at all. That is true of the eastern and western parts of the county of Halifax. Now, the criticism I -would be inclined to make on this resolution is that the line should extend through the county of Guysbo-rough. It appears that the government have thought otherwise. I know that the people who were promoting this enterprise four or live years ago, had a good deal of difficulty because the line did not extend from Upper Musquodoboit through the county of Guysborough. Whether they will be able to overcome that difficulty now, I do not know. I hope they will. But, it seems to me that that is a valid criticism upon this project. If the votes provided for in the first and fourth resolutions were consolidated so that we would have a trunk line from Halifax to the eastern part of the province, it seems to me that the project would be improved. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals will see, that with the present line running along the south side of Nova Scotia from Yarmouth to Halifax, and continuing from Halifax to Guysborough we would have not only a line along the north side of the province, from Yarmouth to Halifax, running through Pictou and Cape Breton by way of the Intercolonial Railway, but along the south side of the province we would have exactly the same thing. But, you stop this line of railway from Upper Musquodoboit at forty miles, and you stop it at a place which has no great population, and which has no particular merits as a terminal point, although it might afford some local traffic to a line running through. That is the difficulty about the successful carrying out of the project before the committee, although I regard it as some measure of comfort for the county of Halifax.

Mr. Chairman, I have to add my support to what has been already said. It is quite true that a longer railway might have been of greater advantage, but the people of the valley probably decided that it would be more advantageous to them to undertake that which it was in their means to accomplish, rather than to have a longer and more ambitious line which might be longer delayed in its completion. The people of the valiey are cut off entirely from communication, and in consequence of

the want of communication with the sea or with lines of railway, their products are of comparatively little value to them. A large number of the more active young men of the district have left. The people of the valley have done all they could. They have endeavoured to get companies to construct the road, and they are supporting the project to the utmost of their ability. The Nova Scotia government has aided in the work of subsidizing the road to an extent equal to that which is asked from this government. Now, I think from these considerations, fulfilling all the requisites laid down by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), there will be no difficulty on the part of hon. gentlemen on either side of the House supporting this very necessary undertaking. It will add materially to the revenue of the Intercolonial Railway, because the road does not run parallel with the Intercolonial Railway, but it brings a certain portion of the country into connection with,the Intercolonial at Windsor Junction. It runs diagonally to the Intercolonial Railway, and will tap a large district contributing materially to the revenue of the Intercolonial Railway. I give my cordial support to this vote.
For a line of railway from Pubnico, Nova Scotia, to Port Clyde or Clyde River, in lieu of the unexpended balance of subsidy by 1897, chap. 4, sec. 2, paragraph 29, not exceeding thirty-one miles, $99,200.

This is part of the through line which the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has just mentioned, as running from Halifax to Yarmouth, on the South Shore. In 1897 we subsidized sixty-one miles of this line from Yarmouth to Port Clyde. Thirty miles have been built and the subsidy has been earned. Twenty miles more have been built, and partially operated, though I think it is not in technical operation to-day. These twenty miles, together with the remainder of that grant, will lapse unless renewed, but it is part of a large through line to which The government of Nova Scotia are granting very special and exceptional aid. The sections of the road which have been hitherto constructed, and the sections which will be built, will form an enterprise which I think will find favour in the country.

I can tell the hon. gentleman from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) that the country through which this railway runs is described as the richest part of the province for producing timber, and by reason of its mineral resources.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I have no doubt at all that this line will within a reasonable period, be a line that will accommodate a very great deal of traffic. The southern shore of the province has become more and more accessible to American tourists, and they are flocking there in the *summer in very great numbers. I think it |
will have the same success that the Cape Breton railway had in that respect.
To the Toronto, Lindsay and Pembroke Railway Company, for a line of railway from the western terminus of the twenty miles subsidized by 1889, chap. 7, sec. 2, paragraph 47, westerly towards Bancroft, not exceeding twenty miles, in lieu of the subsidy granted by 1900, chap. 8, sec. 2, paragraph 3 ; also from the terminus of previously subsidized lines at a point about forty miles west from Golden Lake westerly to Bancroft, not exceeding eleven miles; in all not exceeding thirty-one miles, $99,200.

The history of this road is this. By 56 Victoria, chapter 98. of the province of Ontario, the Pembroke Southern Railway was incorporated to build a line from Pembroke to Douglas, and by 59 Victoria that Act was amended so as to allow the company to construct their line from Pembroke to Golden Lake. In 1897 the Dominion government granted a subsidy of $3,200 per mile to aid in the construction of the railway. That has been built, the subsidy earned and paid over, and the road is now in successful operation. By 62 Victoria (1899) the Ontario legislature incorporated the Toronto, Lindsay and Pembroke Company for the purpose of building from the terminus of the Pembroke Southern Railway to Bancroft in the county of Hastings, a distance of fifty-one miles. Application was made for a subsidy to the Dominion government, and by 02-63 Victoria, assistance was granted for twenty miles. Under 03-64 Victoria, further subsidy was granted to the line between Golden Lake and Bancroft, but the wording of that grant was defective and it was doubtful whether we could caiTy out the intention of the Act. The latter of the subclause read :
From the western terminus of the twenty miles subsidized by chap. 4 of the Act of 1899, for a distance not exceeding twenty miles.
The twenty miles subsidy given by chapter 4 of 1897, was given to the Pembroke Southern Railway, and this subsidy was earned and paid over before any vote was really made for the road between Golden Lake and Bancroft. This resolution is passed for the purpose of substituting it in lieu of what was intended by the previous vote, and in order to remove the doubt which was entertained by the Railway Department, and by the Department of Justice and by the company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Docs the minister think he is complying with the law in voting money in that way.
Quite so. They have gone on upon the assurance that we would correct what was an uncertainty about it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I wish to say that this will form another new route from Ottawa to the west. It is all right.

For a line of railway from Chipman Station, N.B., to Gibson, in lieu of the subsidies granted by 1897, chap, 4, and 1899, chap. 7, sec. 2, paragraph 31, not exceeding forty-five miles, $144,-
000.

This is a revote of a grant which was made from Chipman Station-adjacent to the Newcastle coal mine, the only coal we know of in the province of New Brunswick situated in the county of Queen's-to Gibson which is a point opposite the city of Fredericton on the St. John river. This forty-five miles would be an extension of the line towards the St. John river to a point immediately opposite Fredericton.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is this the same line for which a subsidy has been voted by the local government ?

Exactly the same.
To the Inverness and Richmond Railway Company for a line of railway from a point at or near Point Tupper on the Intercolonial Railway, to Broad Cove and Cheticamp, Nova Scotia, in lieu of the subsidies, granted by 1897, chap. 4, 1899, chap. 7, sec. 2, paragraph 29, and 1900, chap. 8, sec. 2, paragraph 27, not exceeding ninety-eight miles, $313,600.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This is a gathering up of several sections of road which have been voted subsidies from time to time, and consolidating them in one vote. The proposed road starts from the Intercolonial Railway at the Strait of Canso and runs along northward on the coast of the county of Inverness passing through a very good farming section, and also through valuable coal fields. It runs to the shire town of Port Hood, thence to Mabou, on to Broad Cove, which has one of the most valuable coal deposits in the province, and up to the very large French fishing settlement of Cheticamp. The road was built from Port Hastings as far as Port Hood, and I think they are rapidly extending the whole work.
I thought this road was nearly finished.

Some parts of the subsidy has actually been paid and of course this is for the balance.
For a line of railway from Caplin to Paspebiac, Quebec, in lieu of subsidy granted by 1899, chap. 7, sec. 2, paragraph 15, the subsidy contract to be entered into with the trustees or receivers under mortgage from the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company, and to contain the conditions that the subsidy when earned shall be paid in the following manner :-
1st. To the Hamilton Bridge Works Company in payment for bridge superstructures on the said section of railway, when furnished and erected by that company, not to exceed $35,000.
2nd. For the completion of the road-bed and works incidental thereto.

3rd. Towards payment of overdue balances, pro rata, in settlement of claims for labour, boarding-house claims, and material and supplies furnished in connection with the construction of the said section of railway; in all not exceeding thirty miles, $96,000.
This is a subsidy framed in a special way. It is a revote, and it has already been passed upon by parliament. It is an extension to Paspebiac of what is known as the Baie des Chaleurs Railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The Atlantic and Lake Superior ?

The Atlantic and Lake Superior, as it is now called. We have asked that this subsidy be paid under certain conditions. First, the Hamilton Bridge Company are to be paid, on furnishing the bridge, a sum not exceeding $35,000. This road has been- under construction, and I think has been pretty well completed down to within about three miles of Paspebiac ; but, although the subsidy was alive, yet, by reason of difficulties connected with the organization of the company, and by reason of the credit of the company not being what might be desired, the bridge company, before they would proceed with the construction of the bridge, required some assurance that they would be paid for the bridge out of the subsidy, if a renewal of the subsidy were granted by parliament.
Mi-. WALLACE. Is the railway company a consenting party ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes. Then, there are the three miles, or whatever may remain of the rest of the thirty miles to be completed before the subsidy is earned; and whatever it may cost to complete this shall be paid next in order out of this subsidy. If there is any balance of the subsidy after that, it will go to liquidate the claims of labourers, persons who have furnished supplies, boardinghouse keepers, and others.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Suppose the boarding-house keepers have nothing coming to them, are you going to go hawking around for second or third claims ?
No. We have already claims from these people filed. No doubt a great many of them are just and honest claims, and ought to be paid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: After you settle the claim of a labourer, you should let him go and settle his own board bill.
We will take care that two people are not paid for the same bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There is nothing set out here to show what class of claims shall be

paid. In the first place, I think you are establishing a very had precedent by voting subsidies to railways that have claims standing against them; because you will have plenty of applications of the same kind. I could understand it if you specified that only legal claims would be paid.
The hon. gentleman would not suggest that we should provide in the Bill to pay legal claims. We will not pay claims which are illegal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My hon. friend would not say that we should have judgments of the court before we would pay claims of labouring men amounting to $20 or $25.
I say you are laying down a bad precedent. In granting charters we always stipulate that claims established by the courts shall be paid.

This road has been in a most unfortunate position. It is the old Baie des Chaleurs Railway, which has been reorganized as the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway. The people of Gaspe need this railway very badly. Three or four years ago the railway was granted a subsidy for an extension from Caplin to Paspebiac. A good deal of work has been done by the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company, but it has not paid its bills, and is insolvent, and trustees have taken possession of the road. We make provision that they will complete the road, but they are not to touch a single dollar of the subsidy which we are voting except what they shall earn. All the money which goes to complete the road shall be paid to the parties who do the work, and after that, if there is a balance, the intention is to pay the outstanding claims of workmen and others. The Minister of Railways has in his hands a number of these claims.
Have they all been filed ?

I do not know. Perhaps there may be some which have not been filed. But I know that the Minister of Railways has in his hands claims for overdue bills for wages, accounts for board, materials, provisions furnished, and so forth. It is intended to do the best we can with the balance of the money-to distribute it pro rata among all these creditors. I do not know that we could have done anything better than that.
I do not understand the clause in the first paragraph: ' the subsidy when earned.' Is the money to be advanced on progress estimates, or when the road is finished ?
They have to finish the thirty miles of road.
That will remove a good deal of the*difficulty.

This railway runs through the county of Bonaventure, which I have the honour to represent, and the subsidy covers thirty miles from Caplin to Paspebiac, which means reaching deep water. There is a fine harbour at Paspebiac, where boats can come in during ten mouths in the year, and I suppose the government will before long give us a good wharf to accommodate them. The road runs to within three miles of Paspebiac, and it has been operated for the English bondholders since July last, with the exception of three or four days of the heaviest storms of last winter, and the men who have operated the road during that time have been paid regularly. Next we shall attempt to have a company organized, either by these bondholders or trustees, to have the road continued down to Port Daniel, which is the last parish in Bonaventure, and ultimately to GaspS Basin, for which a subsidy has already been voted. As the right hon. the Prime Minister has said, the county has been most unfortunate. The road was first started in 1885, under the name of the Baie des Chaleurs Company. Then it was transferred to the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company. In July last the company became insolvent, its time checks are scattered all over the country, very few of the labourers have been paid, and they are clamouring for their wages, and this solution which the government is bringing about is the only solution possible of one of the most entangling railway messes on record in the history of Canada.

I must make another appeal for the correspondence. In the case of the subsidy to the Inverness and Richmond Railway Company, there must be a good deal of correspondence in connection with the negotiations for the securing of that subsidy. There must also be a lot of correspondence in connection with the subsidy No. 9. Surely these papers ought to be on the Table.
There has not been any correspondence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is impossible.
There has been an application by the trustees.

There must be correspondence relating to both these subsidies. There could not have been this arrangement made with the trustees of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company unless there was correspondence, and that correspondence should be put on the Table. Why should we have to wait until the subject comes up before we can get the information we require. I want the applications and all the papers with reference to these subsidies so that I can read them myself.

We have reached now the 9th subsidy, and we have not seen a



single paper laid on the Table. Some one put a map on the Table and explained it and that is all the information given us. We are entitled to have all the documents and correspondence. In this case of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company, the minister says there is no correspondence.
Not a particle.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Does he mean to tell us that before giving a subsidy to a road In which so many conflicting interests were concerned, there were no negotiations and correspondence ? That is imposing on our credulity a little too much. The power is given the minister to say what claims for labour, for board, for supplies, and; materials furnished in connection with the construction of the line of railways from Caplin to Paspebiac shall be paid and how they shall be paid, and yet he tells us that he has no correspondence or other documents to lay before us. I think the right hon. the First Minister stated that claims had come in. These claims are in the possession of the government and we are entitled to all the information that justifies the vote we are asked to give.
We are rushing these subsidies through with railroad speed, without a tittle of information. The government refuses to give us the papers, but come down in the last days of the session and ask us to vote millions of dollars without our being put in possession of any data which will enable us to vote intelligently. For my part I must enter my protest.
Last year we voted millions of dollars in a similar way. We voted a subsidy, for instance, to the Rainy River Railway, which is practically a parallel line to the Canadian Pacific Railway, from Winnipeg to Port Arthur or Fort William. The country through which it passes is not worth considering in the light of traffic, and the road can only be considered as connecting the city of Winnipeg and the Georgian Bay ports, so that it is immaterial whether both these roads -are built ten or fifty miles distant from each other, they are practically parallel lines. No doubt some of these subsidies are most justifiable, but I say that we should have special justification for every vote of a railway subsidy, and not simply be asked to rote the money on the general principle that Ihe line is going to benefit somebody or some portion of the country. My experience and observation bear me out in saying that these subsidies often go largely into the hands of bonus hunters and speculators.
It does not reach the people, and is not intended to benefit the people. The money is largely squandered, and they say that some of it goes back to where it started from, instead of being used for the interest of the public.
