House in committee on Bill (No. 67) to incorporate the Quebec Terminal and Railway Company.-Mr. Malouin.
On section 1,

This Bill contains the proposition I referred to this afternoon. The Quebec Bridge Company, which has been so largely subsidized, is to turn over to a subsidiary company, as I understand the Bill, the right to build a road between the end of the bridge and the city of Quebec and around the city. And, under this Bill, this private company-not the bridge company- will control the railway entrance into the city of Quebec along the shore of the river. There is only sufficient land there for one road, and I believe that provision ought to be made whereby the rail traffic which is expected to come from the west and the traffic from the Intercolonial Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway on the south, if it wishes to cross to Quebec, should be given the best means of access to the city. This road ought to be in the hands of the public and not in the hands of a private corporation. I would like the government to give their views in regard to having a private company get possession of this most important entrance into the port of Quebec.

My impression is, and I think I am right, that the Quebec Bridge Company already possesses the powers which are here granted to this new company. The only new power granted here to this company is the power to contract with the Quebec Bridge Company to enter the city. I may say that in this instance, as in many instances in the present session, when a Bill has been carefully considered by the Railway Committee, unless there are strong reasons given to the contrary, the policy I would advocate would be that of supporting the views of the Railway Committee. I have not looked into the case for a long time, but I think that all the powers given to the company are contained in clause 7 :
The company may lay out, construct and operate, by steam, electricity, or other power, a railway of the gauge of four feet eight and one-half inches from a point at or near the northern terminus of the Qubec bridge in the parish of St. Poye to the city of Quebec, and from the southern terminus of the Quebec bridge to a point at or near the point of intersection of the Grand Trunk Railway with the Intercolonial Railway at ChaudiSre Curve, in the county of Ldvis, or at any point on the Grand Trunk Railway to the east thereof.
But the company shall not exercise the powers conferred by this section unless and until the Quebec Bridge Company (which is hereby authorized and empowered so to do), has signified in writing its assent to the exercise by the company of such power^ of construction and operation.

With regard to the entrance to the city of Quebec, I do not admit, as represented by my hon. friend, that there is only one entrance into the city. There is already an entrance by the way of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Charlevoix Railway. They have power to bring their railways to the Champlain market, where there are two railways. It is intended that there should be a common station at the Champlain market, which is just opposite the Frontenac Hotel to-day, one coming from the west and the other from the east.

I desire to ask the right hon. gentleman if, when the original company was chartered to build this bridge, the government retained some kind of control over the tolls and over the running arrangements in return for the immense subsidies which have been voted by this parliament, by the province, and also. I believe, by the city.
I cannot say at this moment, but I am quite sure power is retained over the tolls.
The company had power to build this terminal road in the original charter.
I understand so.

The committee took good care to incorporate in this Bill two sections of the Railway Act which give control to the government over the rates that can be charged by this company, and compel the company to grant equal facilities in every regard to all railroads that wish to use this road.
That was not in the original Bill.

When this was before the Railway Committee, I was interested in having it referred to a special committee, which brought in much needed amendments. There is just one point that I think might be improved in the Bill, and to which I draw the attention of the First Minister. I think he misunderstood my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) in speaking of the one entrance. What he meant was the entrance between the cliffs and the river. There is only room for one railway there. When the Crow's Nest Pass Railway charter was being granted, there was supposed to be just room enough for one track between the mountain side and a little lake in the pass, and we remember the discussion that took place on the necessity of granting running powers over the Crow's Nest Pass Railway to any other road. The reason that I wanted this Bill safeguarded is this : I hope it will not be many pears until the whole space up as far as Wolfe's Cove, in Quebec, will be provided, not with the old shipping docks of timber, which I suppose have disappeared, but with 174J
modern docks for the reception of steamships, where they can receive and disembark freight. In that case, there being a very narrow passage there between the cliff and where the railways must necessarily end, one can readily see that a road controlling one, or at most two tracks along there, would have the whole of that great traffic more or less at its mercy. It is found to be so in many great cities. Take Chicago, for instance. The Transfer Railway Company there actually holds the freight traffic of the great west at its mercy, or did until the matter was controlled a short time ago. I would suggest that, as in the Crow's Nest Pass charter, precaution was taken that running powers should be given over that line to any other company under the jurisdiction of the Governor in Council, or of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, so I maintain that precaution should be taken here so that the company might not be able to favour one railway or individual more than another, when Quebec has become a big shipping port, as I trust it will. Therefore, would it not be advisable that this matter should be absolutely controlled, that the company should have no power to favour one railway more than another, and thereby delay, for instance, to bring in cars from one company.
That is provided for.

I am not sure that it is provided that running powers may be given to other roads. I admit tlierd* is a provision that it shall be subject to order in council. But supposing they come and make all sorts of excuses to the Railway Committee and say : We have only one engine, and we cannot attend to all these matters, and we could not possibly get the cars out of that elevator, or on to that dock in time that the freight might be placed on the ship before it sailed. I am only pointing out what may arise if Quebec becomes a great shipping port. I do not oppose the Bill, but in the interest of the Quebec harbour and of the public, I want this company carefully controlled as it was in the case of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway.

I think the clause which has been adopted will answer all the purposes intended by my hon. friend. This is the new section which has been added by the Railway Committee :
lla. Sections 17 and 18 of chapter 98 of the statutes of 1887 shall apply, mutatis mutandis, to the company and all its undertakings, franchises and facilities, and equal rights and privileges shall be enjoyed by all other companies over and upon the company's railway and all its facilities.
Should there not be some penalty provided or some means whereby the government could compel that being done ?
I think the court can enforce it.
The Railway Committee of the Privy Council has power to enforce it.

But a private company can get control of a terminal road, as has happened In some of the big cities of the States, where they have had all the roads at their mercy, notwithstanding some such provision as this. There is a terminal railway which controls two bridges at St. Louis and which is master of the situation there.
No, their engines are obliged to haul trains of another company.

Yet that terminal railway is one of the grievances at St. Louis. This is an important point. We have no national railways in this country except a small portion of one, but it is a most valuable asset. The easiest thing towards establishing a national system of railways is for the state to control and own an entrance into every great centre. If the entrance !into the cities passes into the hands of a corporation and the public is not protected, then great Injury may be done to the public and to that particular city. I trust that the greatest care will be exercised by the government in regard to this ; and I hope the premier and the Minister of Railways and Canals will make some additional provision. (If it is not done in this House, I hope it will be done in the Senate before the Bill is finally passed.

As an instance, take the great harbour of Montreal, in which the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) Is so much interested; every one who knows anything about that harbour knows that one of the greatest drawbacks to shipping there is the fact that railway trains can only go to the docks during the night. The Grand Trunk Railway Company moves a train, or possibly two or three trains, down there to unload during the night, and if the cars are not unloaded before daylight, it has to haul them two or three miles out to the yards, and wait until after sundown. At Quebec, if ships are billed to sail on a certain day, and the trains of the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canada Atlantic Railway, the Quebec and Lake St. John and the Great Northern, all want to get to the wharfs and there is only one track and one set of engines to haul the cars, it is the easiest thing in the world, if the terminal company wants to favour one railway company more than another, to block almost completely for hours the freight of one line while permitting the other to be loaded on the vessels. That is the only point that I want safeguarded. If these other companies had the right to run their cars and engines on the road, I am satisfied the harbour of Quebec will be greatly benefited,
and that it will become a great port, but, if there is a loop hole, rest assured that these people will take advantage of it, or will bleed the railway companies accordingly.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) is perfectly right in what he says, but he will find that this has been entirely provided for in the Bill. This company is subjected to the provisions of the general railway Act under section 240, as amended, which provides that the railway company must grant every facility to any forwarder of freight, it does not matter whom. The Railway Committee of the Privy Council has absolute power to control this matter. But, there is a further safeguard. It is expressly provided by this Bill that the company shall not grant any facilities to one company that it does not grant to another.
Suppose it does an injustice, how would you rectify it ?

It is under the control of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, which has power to deal with it. In addition to that, the Governor in Council has control of the rates, and has power to fix the maximum rates that will be charged by this company. If the Governor in Council has power to fix the maximum rates charged by this company, and if the Railway Committee of the Privy Council has power to see that the company shall grant equal facilities to every railway or transportation company, it seems to me that the Railway Committee of the House has been most careful in guarding against every possible trouble that might suggest itself to the mind of any hon. gentleman.

Suppose that the engines of this terminal company failed to deliver, or to take away from the dock, cars in a reasonable time; is there any provision whereby the government, or the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, might step in and say that the engines of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the Grand Trunk Railway, shall have running powers over the road 1

Section 240 of the Railway Act is exactly the same as section 2 of .the original English Railway Act of 1854, which has been amended by the Act of 1888, I think. There have been several decisions under both the original section and the present section as amended, and these decisions have defined expressly what the company must do. The railway commissioners in England who have the same powers of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council here, have power, if additional engines are required to handle the business of the public to order the same, and so the Railway Committee of the Privy Council here has power to order the same, and if the order of the Railway Committee is not obeyed,

any person interested may come to the Supreme Court of Canada and have the order of the Railway Committee made an order of said court, and have it enforced by mandamus or injunction.
Why not have a provision in this Bill similar to that in the Crow's Nest Pass Bill, giving other roads the right to run over the road.
I think you have it in the Bill already.
To allow the engines of other companies to run over the road ?
Certainly.
It says that this company shall grant to a company the same facilities as it grants to any other company.

Section 11a is as follows :
Sections 17 and 18 of chapter 98 of the statutes of 1887 shall apply, mutatis mutandis, to the company and all its undertakings, franchises and facilities, and equal rights and privileges shall be enjoyed by all other companies over and upon the company's railway and all Its facilities.
It seems to me that my hon. friend's views are entirely met.
Supposing that the equal rights are very narrow ?

Well, then, my hon. friend will have to write to the World and ask to have an agitation over it.

Mr. MACLEAN moved the third reading Bill (No. 128) for the relief of Lilias Middleton.

I want to emphasize in this particular case what I said on the motion which I made in the earlier part of the session in reference to this question of divorce. If there ever was a case in which the grounds of relief were beyond controversy it is this case. You can hardly conceive of a case in which the proof was easier than in this one, and yet this woman, unfortunately linked to a bad man, and having just ground for the dissolution of the marriage tie, is put to an expense, exclusive of what she paid her own lawyer, amounting to $458 in actual disbursements. That is an example of the difficulty of persons of limited means obtaining redress in cases where the law of the land concedes redress shall be granted. Without enlarging the ground on which divorce is to be
obtained, but simply in a case in which we all concede divorce is warranted, the expense is practically a bar to many persons.
Is it the pleasure of the House that this Bill shall be read a third time now ?

On division.
Motion agreed to on division, and Bill read the third time, and passed.

Somewhere between King and Newmarket. I have not the knowledge of the locality to enable me to say just at what point. I have not the knowledge of the locality which would enable me to do that. Perhaps the hon. gentleman might know himself.

Somewhere between these two points.

The vote before was for a railway run by electricity ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Whatever may be the intention, they have not yet made any statement of that kind to the government, and the subsidy, when voted before, was voted in the ordinary way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has the hon. minister laid on the Table the papers he promised this morning about the extra subsidy given the three railways ?
We will have them on Monday.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister whether this is to be an electric road, or whether the company has the power to make it an electric road. I wish to know whether, under the wording of this vote, the company will have power to run an electric road in connection with the Metropolitan railway which runs through Newmarket. I think that the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart) was correct in saying that the first intention was that the road should be run by electricity.

That question has not yet arisen in connection with this railway any more than with any other railway. If the promoters desire that the road should be run by electricity, that would have to be considered when the contract is entered into, but matters have not reached that stage yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:

speechtext: We now have this information. It was not to embarrass the Minister of Railways that we asked for it. If the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) were here we might have got the information more easily. The minister himself probably knows something about this company and what it tried to do this past year. They tried in the night to connect their line with that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and were only stopped toy the interference of the police. But even the Railway Committee of the Privy Council werq prepared to assist them in carrying out what they had in view. It was directly against the interests of the city of Toronto and against the interests of the people who live on Yonge street. The greatest thoroughfare in Canada is Yonge street, leading from the city of Toronto to Simcoe. This company, controlled by Mr. Warren, having got a franchise for an electrice line on that road proposed to put an electric motor weighing about a hundred tons on the line to run up and down that street, which is a great thoroughfare for farmers and teamsters of all kinds. This is a road in which the constituents of my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Wallace) and my own arei very much interested. We simply wanted to let our constituents know who are the men making the application and whether the construction of the road is now going on. I believe the work is ready to be undertaken and would like to ask the minister whether the plans have been approved of ?
The plans have been sent back from here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Approved ?
I do not know whether they were finally approved or not. I do not think the order in coucil has been passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The subsidy will not apply until the plans were approved ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The extraordinary thing about this is that the resolution says that they may start to build a road any place between King and Newmarket. These two points are about twelve miles apart, and the railway which is allowed to start anywhere within twelve miles is to be fifteen Mr. BLAIR.
miles long. Now, the minister tells us that they have approved the location of the line. Then we want to know that location. Is it to start at King station, or at Aurora, or Newmarket, or some point between ?
I think the subsidy for this electric road-it is an electric road is it not?
I have no information to that effect.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This road runs through one of the best cultivated and most thickly settled sections of the county of York. And I think it is a shame for the Dominion of Canada to give a bonus to build a road through that country. I think the government does not thoroughly understand the question, or they would not be led into such a trap. They are laying themselves open to one of the greatest scandals in the country. If these people cannot build a road through that section and make it pay, they had better not have anything to do with railways. I will stay here all night before I would vote! this subsidy. I think it is a down right shame.
Is this an electric or a steam railway ?

I have heard to-night for the first time the suggestion that it is to be an electric road. We have never given a subsidy, and, so far as I am concerned, never will give a subsidy to aid the construction of a tramway or electric railway in this country. We have not done it, and it is not proposed to do it by this vote. If these people choose to construct an electric railway and run it by electricity, they will not get their subsidy, that is all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: They will not need it, because it will run through an excellent country.
There are many railroads that are being projected through excellent sections of the country.
And still they come here and try to pull the wool over your eyes.

In the absence of the Postmaster General, on whose advice I know this railway had been recommended to the government for a subsidy, I beg to say that it does supply a portion of country that is without any railway communication. I believe it is fifteen or nineteen miles from any railway station where this road proposes to go, although it passes through the county of York, which is supposed to have great railway facilities. I know the Postmaster General has taken a great deal of interest in this road.

The fact that the same company owns the electric railway that is running past Bond Bake up to Aurora, rather suggests the possibility or probability that they intend it to be the same kind of railway.
Of course, they would not get the bonus if it was an electric railway.
They will get no subsidy for an electric railway. We are not going to open the door to such applications as that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: From the reading of that letter it is suggested that they intend to build an electric railway. There is another thing about it. The resolution says it shall start from a point between King and Newmarket and run to Schomberg. That is not definite enough. It may be the township of King, which reaches within a few miles of Newmarket, or it may be King's Station, which is about ten miles from Newmarket. But, the fact that the corporators of this company are owners of the electric railway that extends from Toronto now to Aurora, suggests, as I have said, the probability that they intend to extend their electric railway that way.
I move that the item granting 848.000 to build the Newmarket and Schomberg road be struck out of the estimates.

Who
seconds it ?
One of the York members will second it.
The Minister of Railways and Canals says he is not going to open the door to give subsidies to roads run by electricity.
No, tramways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman said railroads. Only a few minutes ago we passed a charter for one of the most important roads in Canada, according to public opinion. The work on the Quebec Bridge and Terminal Railway Company is to be done by electricity, if I understood the Bill rightly. You give a bonus to the Quebec bridge. Mr. Booth, when he contemplated this road in the first place, intended to run it by electricity. I hope, in a short time, to see every railroad in Canada run by electricity, and there is no reason whatever why a bonus should not be given to such roads. I think the Railway Act contemplates roads run by electricity as well as by steam. But, certainly we have already passed an Act a few minutes ago giving power to run by electricity all the terminals for the different railroads that enter Quebec.

The Quebec bridge may be worked by electricity, but it is not contemplated just now to do so. I do not know how it may be later. The time may come when cars on these railways may be run by electricity. But, what my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals, had in his mind was, these cheap tramways, when he said they should not be subsidized.

The government has always made a wide distinction between a tramway and a steam railway. Steam railways are allowed to bring their rails in free of duty, while tramways have to jjay duty on their rails. This subsidy is being voted on the assumption that it is a steam railway to be connected with the Grand Trunk Railway at a point between King and Newmarket.

What alarms me is the idea of saying that the parliament of Canada will be prepared to grant aid to anybody who constructs electric tramways all over this country, or street railways, or railways that are not of the ordinary character of steam railways, such as we have been subsidizing in the past. Perhaps the time may come when some particular undertaking which is to be run by electricity may have claims that parliament may judge wise to accede to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Shall the resolution be adopted ?
Are you going to rut my amendment ?
It is not an amendment.
I have a right to utter my protest against this subsidy. I have moved an amendment, and if it is not in order I want to know it.

If my hon. friend wants to have a division upon his amendment, he can call for a division. The question is put now. whether the item shall be carried or not. It is open to the hon. gentleman to ask a division upon it if he chooses.
I will ask for a division. I think it is time we put a stop to this thing.

For as wild-cat a scheme as ever was proposed to this parliament. Years ago parties came to this parliament Mr. SPROULE.
for a subsidy for a railway, not just exactly on the line of this one, but in the same locality ; and Sir John Macdonald strongly took the ground, which is equally strong to-day, that if this road were going to improve the value of the timber lands and timber up there, which was the chief argument used, the applicants should go to the legislature of Ontario and to the lumbermen whose timber limits would be so largely increased in value. This country is one which we hear boomed a good deal now ; but anybody whoi has gone along the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and has seen the character of the country it goes through knows that it will never amount to anything as a farming country except perhaps in some isolated spots. By going a little further on, settlers can get on the prairie lands of the North-west a farm ready to occupy and to put the plough in without a day's delay, and they will hardly be likely to spend a lifetime among the rocks and stones of this country, attempting to cut down the timber and clear the land and hew out a home in the wilderness, especially as all they get of the pine are the stumps, the lumbermen getting all the trees. I wish for one to enter my protest against the voting away of the money of the people of Canada on such schemes as this.

Personally, like my hon. friend, I am not in favour of railway subsidies, but there are two principles that govern me in supporting these resolutions. This company got into financial difficulties and the road fell into the hands of the bondholders, and has been controlled by them ever since. I would like to point out the need that exists for an air line from the capital to Kingston, or Napanee, or some other point on the Grand Trunk Railway. At present the connection between Ottawa and all southern and western Ontario is dependent on the Canadian Pacific Railway between here and Toronto, which only runs |two trains a day, and runs them at very low speed. I believe that the government, if they wish to make Ottawa more accessible, as it ought to be, to the people of southern and western Ontario, should give a subsidy of some kind for an air line from here to the Grand Trunk Railway. That is not in the interests of Toronto, but of the whole of southern Ontario, and all west and north of Toronto. We want to get the advantage of all those trains that the Grand Trunk Railway are now running between Montreal and the west. The Grand Trunk Railway Is running three or four expresses a day along that route, and the route is double tracked, and the best railway line in the country. It is high time that that splendid system was connected with Ottawa. Here is a subsidy which may help the Kingston and Pembroke road, but does not give connection between Ottawa and the Grand Trunk Railway. There is first-class connection between Montreal and the capital, but between Ottawa and southern and western Ontario there is a lack of railway communication, and I hope that the hon. minister will be prepared to treat in a liberal way a proposal to build from Ottawa, connecting with the Grand Trunk system. As it is, the means of getting from here to Brockville, Kingston, Napanee and Port Hope, and all those towns is very limited.

If the hon. member will be good enough to turn to item No. 6, he. will see that the line there subsidized brings him from Toronto to Ottawa by the shortest way. going through the beautiful town of Lindsay and the adjacent fine section of country. However, I would support also a project to have an outlet by Kingston. I must apologize for instructing the hon. member for East York in geography, but we have a fast line which will give us connection with Toronto over that road.

My hon. friend is living in the moon. What I want is connection with the Grand Trunk Railway double track and its splendid system of connections east and west, which ought to be in direct touch with the capital, in the same way as Ottawa is now in direct touch with Montreal.
We have not a first-class service between southern and western Ontario and Ottawa.

That is the Very thing which is proposed by the vote to which I have referred. What is the traffic between Ottawa and Toronto over the Grand Trunk Railway ? They formerly had a sleeper from Toronto, but as there was only an odd passenger in it now and again, the company took it off. If one wants to come from Toronto to Ottawa by the Grand Trunk Railway, he has to hang around Brockville and get in here about ten o'clock in the morning. There has never been any great traffic on the Grand Trunk Railway for Ottawa. As I say, 1 am supporting this project, but I do not know that a few members of parliament and deputations coming to Ottawa during this session would support a irailway or pay for double tracking it to connect with the Grand Trunk Railway. I hope it may.

What I am asking for, and the House seems to be seized of it, is to bring the city of Ottawa in touch with the splendid double-track system between Montreal, Toronto and the whole of western Ontario. It is not in touch with it now. There is a large traffic at present, and if it does not come by the Grand Trunk Railway it is because that road does not afford facilities. A straight line from here to Kingston will put this capital in connection with the Grand Trunk system.

For once, I agree in the main with my hon. friend for East York (Mr. Maclean) on this railway question. Two opportunities have been lost by the Grand Trunk Railway, one when they let the Ottawa and Prescott road go, which, I suppose, is the shortest line from Ottawa to the River St. Lawrence. It is run by the Canadian Pacific Railway mainly as a freight line, though there are passenger trains on it.
It is Toronto we want to reach.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I know it. The other opportunity lost by the Grand Trunk Railway was when the Kingston, Smith's Falls and Ottawa was left unbuilt. There is some occult influence, some sinister influence behind the votes that are being asked for by the government, these enormous sums of money to which the government desire to pledge the credit of Canada, for the purpose of enriching millionaire lumbermen and holders of timber limits, without procuring any substantial benefit to the people of Canada.

The hon. gentleman said a few moments ago, when I contended that it was not likely that these parties would be able to build this road for this amount, that they would have the provincial subsidy as well.
They have to make their contract and I suppose the provincial government must make their contract with this company. It it now a Dominion company.
Will the Dominion give the subsidy ?
It might not give it.
We want to know from the bon. Minister of Railways and Canals what subsidies are given by Ontario to this road ?
I do not find that my memorandum contains a note of the amounts of the subsidies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is 7,400 acres of land per mile in blocks, to the Algoma Central Railway Company.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is right, but there is a condition attached that the company shall put so many settlers into the country.
Are they to get something else besides the 7,400 acres of land per mile ?
I would not like to say ; I have sent for the Bill.
Is the whole business of the country to stop because we cannot get information ?	[DOT]

No, go on with the other resolutions.
For a line of railway from Bridgetown, Nova Scotia, to Middleton, in extension of the line subsidized by 1900, chap. 8, sec. 2, par. 28, not exceeding eleven miles, $35,200.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We have already subsidized a road from Bridgetown in Annapolis to Victoria Beach on the Bay of Fundy. This is for an extension of 11 miles which will bring it to a point of junction where it will meet the Nova Scotia Central road. Middleton is quite an important point and is likely to become a railway centre, and instead of making the connection at Bridgetown the desire is to 175
bring it to a point of junction where it will have connection with several roads.
Will this proposed road be on the north side of the Annapolis river ?
The general line runs on the north side of the river, but whether this particular piece is on the north side I am not sure.
Yes, it runs on the north side of the Annapolis river and on the north side of Annapolis Basin to Victoria Beach.
At what point will it intersect the Dominion Atlantic ?

It will intersect the Dominion Atlantic at Middleton and join the Nova Scotia Central at Middleton.
For a line of railway from a point on the Grand Trunk Railway at or near Burk's Falls, Ont., to the Maganetawan river, not exceeding two miles, $6,400.
What is the object of the two miles ?

I may say that this is a very important connection between the railway line and navigation on the Maganetawan river. At the present time some 15,000 people live down the Maganetawan river, and their only means of communication with the railway is by navigation to Burk's Falls. When they get to Burk's Falls they have two miles of very rough road to get over to reach the railway, and all the goods coming in and out have now to be carried by wagon from the railway to the boat. This expenditure of $6,400 will accommodate not less than 15,000 people.
I think the Ontario government has given them $10,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.
How much will it take to build it ?
It is a very expensive branch to build, because there are two bridges to be built across the Maganetawan river.

Carried.
For a line of railway between Halifax and the Central Railway, Nova Scotia, from the end of the 40th miles from Halifax, subsidized by 1900, chap. 8, sec. 2, par. 40, to a junction with the Central Railway, Nova Scotia, not exceeding thirty miles, $96,000.

This is a part of the through line from Halifax to Yarmouth by the South Shore to which reference was made this afternoon. It has been subsidized in sections for the greater part of the road from Halifax to the Nova Scotia Central, which crosses the province between the Bay of Fundy to the Atlantic, is about seventy miles. Two sections



of twenty miles each have already been subsidized. It will run through the county of Halifax, through a portion of the county of Lunenburg, and then connect with the Nova Scotia Central at some convenient point. The particular point of junction is not designated, but the distance between Halifax and the Central will be about 70 miles. With the two sections of twenty miles each, this will about fill in the link.
I think in these various subsidies, covering a period of years, we have a sufficient mileage to build the whole line from Halifax to Yarmouth. The line is regarded as of such importance that the local government have undertaken a policy which has been commended by some hon. members in this House. They have undertaken to loan the company on the whole mileage $10,000 per mile, and take a first mortgage for it. I am not sure but that they may find it necessary to grant some further help. With the money so loaned and the Dominion subsidies, it is hoped that this 200 miles lrom Halifax to Yarmouth will be built at a very early date. This tills in one of the missing links.

I feel it my duty to offer a word or two in reference to this subsidy. Let me refer to a road that has been commenced, and all of the work completed except laying the rails between New Germany and Caledonia on the way to Shelburne ; a road which is most essential to develop the resources of the interior of the country. This is a road that any person would view with satisfaction and consider that the money appropriated and the portion expended on it was commendable and prudent. That road at present stops at New Germany, and some weeks ago I made an appeal to the government in this House to extend that road between Shelburne and New Germany, on which already heavy bridges have been built of the very best material, with dressed stone culverts, the substructure of the bridges from the base to the top of the piers being of the very best material also. I ask that that road from Shelburne to New Germany should be extended to Halifax, as it passes through a section of country that cannot be excelled in any part of the Dominion. The land between New Germany and New Ross is superior to most other lands in the province. This section is now very sparsely settled, simply because the people in that remote district have no opportunity of getting their produce to the market. If the road were extended from New Germany to Halifax it would afford a market either at Halifax or at Boston, via Shelburne by a line of steamers. In consequence of the local government not being in sufficient funds to maintain the roads, these people are now unable to get their products to the market.
Have they no means of communication now ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Only over a very rough road. They are in a measure isolated. If this railway were built as I suggest from New Germany to Foster Settlement and New Ross, to Halifax it would really be an international road, as by a line of steamers from Shelburne to Boston it would be the shortest route by five miles for tourists and others from Halifax to Boston. The road for which we voted a subsidy can be built and those living along the St. Margaret's Bay can be accommodated as well by this road as by the road at present proposed. I am not opposing the shore road by any means, but I say it will not suit all these poor people in the interior who are now suffering for want of communication. This road can follow the head waters of St. Margaret's Bay connecting Hubbard's Cove, Chester, and Chester Basin, and then proceed by the valley of the Gold River to New Ross.
How would it connect with Chester ?

Just one moment, please. Thence could go on through New Ross and through Foster Settlement to New Germany and thence to Shelburne. A portion of that road will go through a most fertile belt of land in the constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, Northern Queen's, Brookfield and Caledonia. I ask in all sincerity that the government should view this matter in a fair and impartial light, and grant that subsidy which is so justly due to the people occupying those remote sections of the country. My personal advantage would be to see the road on the Shore, as I reside on the Shore, and the population is mostly on the Shore, but I want to see the country developed. This could be made a sort of colonization road which would keep the people in the country, so that they might have an opportunity of living at home instead of being expatriated from Canada. I go further and say that these people are entitled to this road for the reason that the eastern portion of the province is eared for by the government; all the roads there are supported by government money, they being government railways. These people for whom I speak are contributing very largely of their means to the support of the railways in eastern Nova Scotia, and west of Halifax should reap some benefit as well as those in the east. I feel that the government, guided by a sense of justice, will make the road I refer to an international route, and take it over as a government work. It will open up a direct communication from Halifax to Shelburne via New Ross, Foster Settlement, New Germany. Pleasant River and Caledonia, and by tap lines at intervals to the sea will give the settlers I refer to and those on the shore all the conveniences required.

Mr, WADE. I shall have to ask to be allowed to say a word in this connection, after the remarks made by the hon. member for Lunenburg. I entirely disagree with him, except as he speaks of the importance of New Germany and New Ross. I know those sections very well, and I would be glad to see them have the advantage of a railway. There is only one way, however, for them to get it, that is, from the Central Railway at New Germany, to the Midland at Windsor. The hon. gentleman wishes to apply the subsidy to a road running through the sparsely settled portion of the province. The road he speaks of would have to run back of Hubbard's Cove, which Is the collecting point for the eastern part of St. Margaret's Bay, and run about twelve miles back of Chester, the Saratoga of Nova Scotia. From there it would pass through a comparatively uninhabited country, a very difficult country in which to build a road, until it reached within twelve or fifteen miles of the Central Railway. [DOT]The other night, when the question of cold storage was up, the hon. gentleman asked the government to provide cold storage ears for the shipment of fish from the county of Lunenburg, which is a very important fishing county, as well as the counties of Queen's and Shelburne ; and one of the important industries served by this road will be the transport of fresh fish from the shores of those counties. After advocating refrigerator cars for that purpose, he now asks that this road shall not be built near the shore where the people are. but back in the country. I dissent from that view entirely. In addition to the towns, there is Ghester Basin, which could not be served except by a branch. Then, there is Gold River, Western Shore, Mahone Bay, Lunenburg and Bridgewater, all of which places the hon. gentleman wishes us to leave, and put the road. back in the interior. I contend that that would be most disastrous, and there would be a general outcry in the country if any such attempt were made.

My hon. friend knows right well that Bridgewater. Mahone Bay. and Lunenburg have communication with the Central Railway ; and the cold storage system and fish that could be gathered along the shore could be done satisfactorily at these places. I omitted to mention that for this entire road from Shelburne to Halifax, I do not think that one dollar would be required to be paid for right of way. So far as I am aware-and I am instructed to say so-through the most fertile belt of Queen's and Lunenburg counties, every one of the landholders is willing to give the right of way free, whereas the route along the shore will probably place us in the position of being taxed to a very great extent for the right of way. We have had experience of that in the case of the Central Railway, for which we were unduly taxed, and which 175}
will be a halter around our necks for a long time. Beside, if this road is to follow the windings and indentations of the coast between Halifax and Shelburne, it will be almost one-third longer than it would be by the route I suggest.
On the contrary, it will be shorter.

My hon. friend speaks of Hubbard's Cove. Let me tell him the route I suggest will give direct communication with the head waters of St. Margaret's Bay and take in Huibbard's Cove, and connect with Chester and Chester Basin, and take the valley of Gold River, and proceed thence to New Ross.

That is impossible.
Mr.. KAULBACH. Then, from this belt line down to the coast no part will be more than 18 miles, and some of these places would have direct communication, they being on the belt line. While I do not object to the shore line, I do object to those people back in the woods being allowed to remain there without railway communication, and being told that they have to be satisfied with their situation as they find it or get out1 of the country. I think it is an injustice.
Do I understand that the hon. gentleman wants two lines through Lunenburg ?
I would be satisfied with two lines rather than see those people kept out in the cold.
So would any man in this House or out of it if he could get them. I am happy to get one.
Is the hon. gentleman not getting two-one known as the government road, and one voted to-day ?
Not at all, except at Port Mulgrave, where two lines run through a corner of the county.
The hon. gentleman knows that the road subsidized to-day almost parallels the Intercolonial.
Excuse me ; it leaves the Intercolonial, and when it reaches Country Harbour it will be fifty or sixty miles from it.
The hon. gentleman might have asked for one of these roads when his party was in power.
I did ask for the road from New Germany to Shelburne, and the subsidy was voted and construction done.

My constituents are interested in this railway, and I agree with the hon. gentleman that I would rather have two roads in my constituency

than not have any ; hut I do not expect to get two roads in a hurry, and X shall he very glad to get one. If the hon. gentleman takes a rule and applies it to the map, he will find that from Halifax to the Central Railway, running near New Germany, is about seventy miles which is the subsidy we have provided for this section. At the same time, if the companies propose to consolidate these various sections into one through line, prefer to keep to the shore instead of going inland, X am bound to say that I would rather see a road on the shore than none at all. We do not propose to tie ourselves up to a route in either direction, but leave that to be decided by the companies on commercial grounds. I hope soon to see a road built to New Germany and run south through Queen's county, and I have no doubt that will be taken up to some extent by the new enterprise. In the meantime, we are glad to get one road, and the second one will come in due course.

But my hon. friend will see that a road from Halifax through New Germany, North Brookfield and Caledonia to Shelburne, will give us a direct route ; and it would be much more useful to the public than the other route. Surely, my hon. friend is not in a position to say that that road can be built, and be as useful for the public generally as the road I suggest from Caledonia, through to Shelburne.
The road from New Germany to Shelburne is under contract at this moment, but the company is not able to carry on the work.
By this you will he shutting them out.

No, I am not.
For a line of railway from a point on the Algoma branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, at or near Bruce Lake Station northerly, to a point at or near Rock Lake, in the district of Algoma, not exceeding nine miles, $28,800.
Where is Rock Lake ?
It is nine or ten miles north of Bruce station.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Who is asking for this ?

Two copper mine companies, which, I understand, are very prosperous, and employ a great many men.
For a line of railway from Roberval, Quebec, westward toward James Bay, not exceeding sixty miles, $192,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There are several large rivers falling from the north and west into Lake St. John. All these rivers make very fertile valleys into which

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
colonists are rapidly going, and the object is to project this railway from Roberval, which is the extreme point of the Lake St. John road, towards James Bay, in the valley of the river.
For a line of railway from a point upon the Stonewall branch or the Selkirk branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway to Icelandic River by way of Gimli, not exceeding thirty-five miles, $112,000.

This is an extension of the Selkirk branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway nuns to West Selkirk, and last year that company built a branch from West Selkirk to tap the south end of Lake Winnipeg for the purpose of establishing a summer resort. This railway will run from the end of that branch up to where six or seven thousand Icelanders have settled. It will be thirty-five miles long, and run through a rich well-wooded country, and enable the settlers to clear up their lands. The local government of Manitoba have had, through their agent, five Icelander delegates from North Dakota, go up there to inspect the lands, and as the result we will have 4,000 or 5,000 people from North Dakota to settle in that district at a very early date.
Is it the Canadian Pacific Railway that will build it ?
Yes.
What kind of timber ?

Spruce, tamarack and white birch.
On section 4,

This section has been found to be necessary by reason of the terms of this grant under the previous Act. When they came to construct their line, they found it would be very much more advantageous not only for the undertaking but in the public interest that, instead of building a new line they should utilize a considerable portion of the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, running their railway from Little Current up the Canadian Pacific Railway at one end and running the Sudbury end from the Canadian Pacific Railway, dividing the 66 miles into, we will say, 30 miles on one end and 36 miles on the other. I believe that with this change there will be a saving of some 7 miles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The two terminals are not the same.

Yes, they are the same. But they are practically two branch lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as it stands now, I would like to change the mileage of the

first from 34 miles to 35 miles and the second from 32 miles to 31 miles. This makes the distance the same, a mile being taken off in one case and added on in the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There are no changes in the other clauses ?

The rest of the resolutions are identical with last year's resolutions.
Resolutions reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 146) to authorize the granting of subsidies in aid of the construction of the lines of railways therein mentioned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
